questions.q: What does the autocorrelation function (ACF) at lag k measure?
options: The correlation between y_t and y_{t−k} after removing the effect of lags 1 to k−1
The average of the series over the last k periods
The variance of the series computed k periods apart
The correlation between y_t and y_{t−k}
questions.answer: The correlation between y_t and y_{t−k}
questions.explanation: ACF at lag k is the simple correlation of the series with its own k-period-lagged values. Removing the effect of the intermediate lags is what the PACF does, which is the most common confusion.

questions.q: What does the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) at lag k measure?
options: The correlation between y_t and y_{t−k} including all indirect effects
The correlation between y_t and y_{t−k} after removing the effects of lags 1 to k−1
The share of the total variance of y_t that is explained by the value at lag k alone
The correlation between y_t and an external predictor at lag k
questions.answer: The correlation between y_t and y_{t−k} after removing the effects of lags 1 to k−1
questions.explanation: PACF isolates the direct relationship between y_t and y_{t−k} by controlling for the intermediate lags. Including indirect effects describes the ordinary ACF.

questions.q: The autocorrelation of any series at lag 0 is always equal to:
options: The variance of the series
questions.explanation: A series is perfectly correlated with itself, so ρ0 = 1. The autocovariance at lag 0 equals the variance, which is why some students pick that option, but the autocorrelation is standardised.

questions.q: For a series of n observations, the approximate 95% significance bounds drawn on an ACF plot are:
questions.explanation: Under white noise, sample autocorrelations are approximately normal with standard error 1/√n, giving bounds of ±1.96/√n. Dividing by n instead of √n makes the bounds far too narrow.

questions.q: For a white noise series, the ACF at lags 1, 2, 3, ... should be:
options: Approximately zero, mostly within the significance bounds
Close to 1 at lag 1 and then decaying slowly over many lags
Large spikes at every seasonal lag
Exactly equal to the PACF values squared
questions.answer: Approximately zero, mostly within the significance bounds
questions.explanation: White noise has no autocorrelation, so sample autocorrelations should be near zero (about 95% inside the bounds). A slowly decaying ACF indicates trend or non-stationarity, not white noise.

questions.q: A plot of autocorrelation coefficients against lag number is called a:
options: Correlogram
Histogram
Scatter-plot matrix
Box plot
questions.answer: Correlogram
questions.explanation: The ACF plot is known as a correlogram. A histogram shows a distribution of values, not correlations across lags.

questions.q: How does the PACF at lag 1 relate to the ACF at lag 1?
options: The PACF at lag 1 is always zero
The PACF at lag 1 is the square of the ACF at lag 1
They are equal
The PACF at lag 1 is always 1
questions.answer: They are equal
questions.explanation: At lag 1 there are no intermediate lags to remove, so partial and ordinary autocorrelation coincide. The PACF is always 1 only at lag 0 (if plotted).

questions.q: Sample autocorrelation coefficients can take values in which range?
options: 0 to +1
0 to infinity
−infinity to +infinity
questions.explanation: Autocorrelation is a correlation coefficient, so it lies between −1 and +1. Negative values are possible, for example when highs tend to follow lows.

questions.q: Which test checks whether a group of autocorrelations (e.g. the first 10 lags) is jointly zero?
options: Augmented Dickey–Fuller test
F-test on a regression slope
Shapiro–Wilk test
Ljung–Box test
questions.answer: Ljung–Box test
questions.explanation: The Ljung–Box (portmanteau) test checks whether several autocorrelations together differ from zero. The ADF test is for unit roots, not joint autocorrelation.

questions.q: The ACF of a monthly sales series starts near 0.95 and decreases very slowly over many lags. This most likely indicates:
options: The series is white noise
The series is non-stationary, typically because of a trend
The series is a stationary MA(1) process with a large positive θ
The series has no autocorrelation
questions.answer: The series is non-stationary, typically because of a trend
questions.explanation: A slow, almost linear decay in the ACF is the classic signature of trend or a unit root. An MA(1) would show a single spike at lag 1 and then cut off.

questions.q: A retailer has 120 monthly sales observations. The sample ACF at lag 3 is 0.15. Using the usual 95% bounds, how should this be read?
options: Significant, because 0.15 is larger than 0.05
Significant, because 0.15 exceeds ±1.96/120 ≈ 0.016
It cannot be judged without first computing the PACF
Not significant, because 0.15 lies inside ±0.179
questions.answer: Not significant, because 0.15 lies inside ±0.179
questions.explanation: The bound is 1.96/√120 ≈ 0.179, so 0.15 is inside it. Comparing with 0.05 confuses a correlation with a p-value, and 1.96/n wrongly narrows the bounds.

questions.q: For the series 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, what is the sample lag-1 autocorrelation r1 (using the standard formula with the overall mean)?
questions.explanation: Mean = 6, deviations −4, −2, 0, 2, 4; the sum of lagged products is 8+0+0+8 = 16 and the sum of squares is 40, so r1 = 16/40 = 0.40. A Pearson correlation of the overlapping pairs would give 1.00, but the ACF uses the full-series mean and variance.

questions.q: The ACF of daily footfall at a Bengaluru mall shows significant spikes at lags 7, 14 and 21. This suggests:
options: Weekly seasonality
An upward trend
An MA(7) process with no seasonality
Monthly seasonality
questions.answer: Weekly seasonality
questions.explanation: Repeating spikes at multiples of 7 in daily data indicate a weekly cycle (weekends vs weekdays). Monthly seasonality would show around lag 30.

questions.q: For a stationary AR(1) process with φ = 0.6, what is the theoretical ACF at lag 2?
questions.explanation: For AR(1), ρk = φ^k, so ρ2 = 0.6² = 0.36. Zero would be the PACF at lag 2, not the ACF.

questions.q: For a stationary AR(1) process with φ = 0.6, what is the theoretical PACF at lag 2?
questions.explanation: An AR(1) has a direct link only to lag 1, so the PACF cuts off after lag 1 and equals 0 at lag 2. 0.36 is the ACF at lag 2.

questions.q: A stationary series shows one significant ACF spike at lag 1 and then nothing, while the PACF decays gradually. Which model is suggested?
options: MA(1)
AR(1)
AR(2)
White noise
questions.answer: MA(1)
questions.explanation: An ACF that cuts off after lag q with a tailing PACF is the MA(q) signature. AR(1) would show the reverse: PACF cutting off and ACF tailing.

questions.q: A stationary series has a PACF with significant spikes at lags 1 and 2 and none after, while the ACF tails off. Which model is suggested?
options: MA(2)
AR(2)
ARMA(2,2)
AR(1)
questions.answer: AR(2)
questions.explanation: A PACF cutting off after lag p with a decaying ACF points to AR(p), here p = 2. MA(2) would have the ACF cutting off after lag 2.

questions.q: After fitting a model to weekly FMCG sales, the Ljung–Box test on residuals (10 lags) gives a p-value of 0.42. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Significant autocorrelation remains in the residuals, so the model must be revised
The series is non-stationary
No evidence of remaining autocorrelation; the residuals look like white noise
The model explains 42% of the variance
questions.answer: No evidence of remaining autocorrelation; the residuals look like white noise
questions.explanation: The Ljung–Box null is that the autocorrelations are jointly zero; p = 0.42 means we fail to reject it, which is what a good model needs. Reading p as a share of variance explained is a common mistake.

questions.q: What does the ACF of a stationary AR(1) process with φ = −0.7 look like?
options: All positive and decaying slowly
A single negative spike at lag 1 and zero afterwards
Alternating in sign while decaying in magnitude
Constant at −0.7 for all lags
questions.answer: Alternating in sign while decaying in magnitude
questions.explanation: ρk = (−0.7)^k, so the values are −0.7, 0.49, −0.343, ... alternating and shrinking. A single spike then zero describes an MA(1).

questions.q: With n = 100, r1 = 0.2 and r2 = 0.1, what is the Box–Pierce statistic Q = n Σ r_k² over the first two lags?
questions.explanation: Q = 100 × (0.2² + 0.1²) = 100 × 0.05 = 5.0. Forgetting to square gives 100 × 0.3 = 30, and forgetting to multiply by n gives 0.05.

questions.q: An analyst sees an ACF that starts at 0.95 and decays very slowly, and a PACF with one large spike near 0.95 at lag 1. What should be the next step?
options: Fit an AR(1) with φ ≈ 0.95 directly to the levels, because the PACF cuts off after lag 1
Test for a unit root (e.g. ADF) and difference the series before choosing ARMA orders
Fit an MA(1) because the PACF has only one spike
Conclude the series is white noise
questions.answer: Test for a unit root (e.g. ADF) and difference the series before choosing ARMA orders
questions.explanation: This pattern indicates a near-unit-root, non-stationary series; ACF/PACF identification is only valid after achieving stationarity. Fitting AR(1) to levels treats a likely random walk as a stationary process.

questions.q: For a stationary series, both the ACF and the PACF tail off gradually with no clear cut-off. What is the best modelling approach?
options: Fit a pure AR model with p set equal to the last PACF lag that crosses the significance bounds
Consider mixed ARMA(p,q) models and compare candidates using AIC/BIC and residual checks
Fit a pure MA model with q equal to the last significant ACF lag
Conclude the series cannot be modelled
questions.answer: Consider mixed ARMA(p,q) models and compare candidates using AIC/BIC and residual checks
questions.explanation: When neither function cuts off, a mixed ARMA process is indicated and orders are chosen by information criteria. Using the last significant lag for a pure model ignores that both functions decay.

questions.q: For a stationary AR(2) process with φ1 = 0.5 and φ2 = 0.3, what is the theoretical lag-1 autocorrelation ρ1 = φ1/(1 − φ2)?
questions.explanation: ρ1 = 0.5/(1 − 0.3) = 0.5/0.7 ≈ 0.714. Using 0.5 assumes ρ1 = φ1 as in AR(1); 0.385 comes from wrongly dividing by 1 + φ2.

questions.q: You plot the ACF of a genuine white noise series for 20 lags with 95% bounds. How many spikes would you expect to fall outside the bounds purely by chance?
options: None
About 1
About 5
About 10
questions.answer: About 1
questions.explanation: With 5% false positives per lag, 20 × 0.05 ≈ 1 spike is expected by chance. Expecting none leads analysts to over-react to a single marginal spike.

questions.q: An e-commerce firm's demand model has residual Ljung–Box p-value of 0.001. What should the planning team conclude?
options: The model is excellent, because a very small p-value means the fitted coefficients are significant
The residuals are white noise, so forecasts are optimal
The model has left predictable structure in the residuals, so it can be improved
The original series must be stationary
questions.answer: The model has left predictable structure in the residuals, so it can be improved
questions.explanation: A small Ljung–Box p-value rejects the null of no autocorrelation, so information remains in the residuals. Treating any small p-value as 'good' is a common misreading.

questions.q: Why is the PACF, rather than the ACF, used to identify the order p of an AR model?
options: The ACF of an AR(p) is always zero beyond lag p
The PACF is easier to compute than the ACF
In an AR(p), correlations beyond lag p are only indirect, passing through intermediate lags; the PACF removes these, so it cuts off at p
The PACF measures seasonality and the ACF measures trend, and because AR models describe seasonal persistence the PACF is the natural tool
questions.answer: In an AR(p), correlations beyond lag p are only indirect, passing through intermediate lags; the PACF removes these, so it cuts off at p
questions.explanation: AR dependence propagates, so the ACF decays rather than cuts off; the PACF strips out indirect effects and cuts off after lag p. Saying the ACF is zero beyond p confuses AR with MA behaviour.

questions.q: A series has ACF ρ1 = 0.8 and ρ2 = 0.64. Using φ22 = (ρ2 − ρ1²)/(1 − ρ1²), what is the PACF at lag 2?
questions.explanation: φ22 = (0.64 − 0.64)/(1 − 0.64) = 0; the pattern is exactly AR(1) with φ = 0.8. Reporting 0.64 confuses the ACF at lag 2 with the PACF.

questions.q: A series has ACF ρ1 = 0.5 and ρ2 = 0.5. What is the PACF at lag 2, using φ22 = (ρ2 − ρ1²)/(1 − ρ1²)?
questions.explanation: φ22 = (0.5 − 0.25)/(1 − 0.25) = 0.25/0.75 ≈ 0.333. Stopping at the numerator gives 0.25; assuming PACF = ACF gives 0.5.

questions.q: After fitting a non-seasonal ARIMA to monthly hotel occupancy, the residual ACF shows one significant spike at lag 12 and nothing else. What does this imply?
options: The model is adequate because only one spike is significant
Seasonality has not been captured; add a seasonal term (e.g. seasonal MA or AR at lag 12)
Increase the non-seasonal AR order to p = 12 so that the model includes every lag up to the seasonal one
The series needs a second ordinary difference
questions.answer: Seasonality has not been captured; add a seasonal term (e.g. seasonal MA or AR at lag 12)
questions.explanation: A residual spike exactly at the seasonal lag signals unmodelled annual dependence, best handled by a seasonal term. Raising p to 12 adds many unnecessary parameters.

questions.q: Why is the ACF of a strongly trending series misleading for identifying short-run dependence?
options: The ACF cannot be computed at all when a trend is present, because the mean of a trending series is undefined
The trend creates large positive autocorrelations at many lags, masking the short-run correlation structure
A trend makes all autocorrelations negative
A trend only affects the PACF, not the ACF
questions.answer: The trend creates large positive autocorrelations at many lags, masking the short-run correlation structure
questions.explanation: Trend dominates the covariance, so the ACF stays high for many lags and hides ARMA structure until the series is differenced or detrended. The ACF can be computed; it is just uninformative.

references: Autocorrelation tells us how strongly a series is related to its own past. The ACF at lag k is the correlation between this period's value and the value k periods earlier, for example this week's sales and sales one week ago. The partial autocorrelation (PACF) at lag k measures only the direct link between today and k periods back, after removing the influence of the lags in between. We plot both as correlograms with significance bounds of about ±1.96/√n. Spikes outside the bounds are meaningful. Together they help us identify models: an AR(p) shows a PACF that cuts off after lag p and an ACF that tails off, while an MA(q) shows the ACF cutting off after lag q.

Think of daily footfall in a mall. If Saturday crowds are high, the following Saturday is probably high too, so the ACF shows spikes at lags 7, 14 and 21, revealing weekly seasonality. If yesterday's footfall strongly predicts today's, we see a big lag-1 autocorrelation. The PACF answers a sharper question: does footfall two days ago still matter once we know yesterday's? If not, the PACF cuts off after lag 1, pointing to an AR(1). A slowly decaying ACF warns us the series has a trend and is not stationary, so we should difference it first. Bars inside the ±1.96/√n bands are treated as noise.

For a manager, the ACF and PACF are diagnostic tools that decide which forecasting model to build and whether a model is finished. Before modelling, we check the ACF: slow decay means non-stationarity, so we difference. Then the patterns guide the order: PACF cut-off suggests autoregressive terms, ACF cut-off suggests moving-average terms, and both tailing off suggests ARMA. After fitting, we check the residual ACF and run a Ljung–Box test. If the p-value is large and no spikes cross the bounds, the residuals are white noise and the model has captured the predictable pattern. Significant spikes, for instance at lag 12, mean money is being left on the table and the model should be improved.

questions.q: In time series modelling, an MA(q) process expresses y_t as:
options: The average of the last q observations of y
A constant plus the current and q past white-noise error terms
A linear function of the q previous values of y plus a white-noise error term
A trend line plus a seasonal index
questions.answer: A constant plus the current and q past white-noise error terms
questions.explanation: An MA(q) model is a weighted sum of current and past random shocks (forecast errors). Averaging the last q observations is moving-average smoothing, and lagged values of y define an AR model.

questions.q: Which equation represents an MA(1) process?
options: y_t = μ + ε_t + θε_{t−1}
y_t = c + φy_{t−1} + ε_t
y_t = y_{t−1} + ε_t
questions.answer: y_t = μ + ε_t + θε_{t−1}
questions.explanation: MA(1) uses the current shock and one lagged shock. c + φy_{t−1} + ε_t is AR(1), and y_{t−1} + ε_t is a random walk.

questions.q: How does the MA component in ARIMA differ from moving-average smoothing of sales data?
options: They are the same technique under different names
MA(q) models dependence on past forecast errors, whereas smoothing averages past observations
MA(q) averages the last q observations with equal weights, whereas smoothing gives more weight to recent observations
Smoothing uses past errors, whereas MA(q) uses past observations
questions.answer: MA(q) models dependence on past forecast errors, whereas smoothing averages past observations
questions.explanation: The MA in ARIMA refers to lagged error (shock) terms, not to averaging observed values. Treating them as the same is a very common confusion.

questions.q: The theoretical ACF of an MA(q) process:
options: Decays slowly and never reaches zero
Cuts off after lag 1 regardless of q
Cuts off (becomes zero) after lag q
Shows spikes only at seasonal lags
questions.answer: Cuts off (becomes zero) after lag q
questions.explanation: An MA(q) only has memory of q past shocks, so autocorrelations beyond lag q are zero. Slow decay is typical of AR or non-stationary series.

questions.q: Is a finite-order MA(q) process stationary?
options: Only if all θ coefficients are less than 1 in absolute value
Only if q is even
Yes, always, for any finite parameter values
Never, because errors accumulate over time
questions.answer: Yes, always, for any finite parameter values
questions.explanation: A finite MA is a finite weighted sum of white noise, so its mean and variance are constant. The |θ| < 1 condition relates to invertibility, not stationarity.

questions.q: An MA(1) process y_t = μ + ε_t + θε_{t−1} is invertible when:
options: θ > 0 only
questions.explanation: Invertibility requires |θ| < 1 so the MA can be rewritten as a convergent infinite AR. Confusing it with stationarity is common; every finite MA is stationary.

questions.q: The error terms ε_t in an MA model are assumed to be:
options: Autocorrelated over time, since the MA model is built to capture that correlation
Increasing over time with the trend
White noise: zero mean, constant variance and uncorrelated over time
Equal to the observed values of the series
questions.answer: White noise: zero mean, constant variance and uncorrelated over time
questions.explanation: MA models are built from uncorrelated shocks; all the autocorrelation in y comes from overlapping shocks. Autocorrelated errors would mean the model is mis-specified.

questions.q: In an MA(q) model, q represents:
options: The number of lagged error terms included
The number of lagged values of y included
The number of differences taken
The seasonal period
questions.answer: The number of lagged error terms included
questions.explanation: q counts lagged shocks. Lagged values of y belong to the AR order p and differences to d.

questions.q: The theoretical PACF of an invertible MA(q) process:
options: Cuts off sharply after lag q
Is zero at every lag
Equals 1 at every lag
Tails off gradually
questions.answer: Tails off gradually
questions.explanation: For an MA process the PACF decays while the ACF cuts off. Cutting off after lag q is the ACF property, not the PACF.

questions.q: What is the mean of the process y_t = μ + ε_t + θ1ε_{t−1} + θ2ε_{t−2}?
options: 0 always
μ
questions.answer: μ
questions.explanation: Each ε has zero mean, so the expected value is just μ. The μ/(1 − ...) form resembles the mean of an AR process.

questions.q: For an MA(1) process with θ = 0.5, what is the lag-1 autocorrelation ρ1 = θ/(1 + θ²)?
questions.explanation: ρ1 = 0.5/(1 + 0.25) = 0.40. Reporting θ itself (0.50) assumes ρ1 = θ, which is an AR(1) habit; 0.67 comes from dividing by 1 − θ².

questions.q: For an MA(1) process with θ = 0.5, what is the theoretical autocorrelation at lag 2?
questions.explanation: An MA(1) has memory of one shock only, so ρ2 = 0. Squaring θ (0.25) or ρ1 (0.16) imports AR(1)-style geometric decay.

questions.q: An MA(1) model for daily branch cash withdrawals is y_t = 100 + ε_t + 0.6ε_{t−1} (₹ lakh). Today's actual was 110 and today's forecast was 100, so ε_t = 10. What is tomorrow's forecast?
questions.explanation: ŷ_{t+1} = 100 + 0.6 × 10 = 106 because the future shock has expected value zero. Using today's actual (110) treats the model like a naive forecast.

questions.q: For the same MA(1) model y_t = 100 + ε_t + 0.6ε_{t−1} with ε_t = 10, what is the forecast two days ahead?
questions.explanation: Two steps ahead both relevant shocks are future values with zero expectation, so the forecast reverts to the mean of 100. 103.6 wrongly applies AR-style decay (100 + 0.6 × 6).

questions.q: An MA(2) model is y_t = 50 + ε_t + 0.4ε_{t−1} + 0.2ε_{t−2}. If ε_t = 5 and ε_{t−1} = 10, what is ŷ_{t+1}?
questions.explanation: ŷ_{t+1} = 50 + 0.4 × 5 + 0.2 × 10 = 54. Using only the first MA term gives 52, and adding ε_t unweighted (50 + 5 + 2) gives 57.

questions.q: A stationary series shows significant ACF spikes at lags 1 and 2 only and a gradually decaying PACF. Which model fits?
options: AR(2)
MA(2)
MA(1)
ARMA(2,2)
questions.answer: MA(2)
questions.explanation: The ACF cutting off after lag 2 with a tailing PACF is the MA(2) signature. AR(2) would need the PACF, not the ACF, to cut off at 2.

questions.q: An MA(1) process has error variance σ² = 4 and θ = 0.5. What is the variance of y_t, given Var(y) = σ²(1 + θ²)?
questions.explanation: Var(y) = 4 × (1 + 0.25) = 5. Forgetting the lagged shock gives 4; using 1 + θ gives 6.

questions.q: What is the maximum possible absolute value of the lag-1 autocorrelation for an MA(1) process?
questions.explanation: ρ1 = θ/(1 + θ²) peaks at 0.5 when θ = ±1. Assuming it can reach 1 ignores that the current shock always adds unshared variance.

questions.q: A hotel's weekly demand changes show a single negative ACF spike of −0.45 at lag 1 and a negative, decaying PACF. Which model is suggested?
options: AR(1) with a negative φ
MA(1) with a positive θ
MA(1) with a negative θ
White noise
questions.answer: MA(1) with a negative θ
questions.explanation: A lone ACF spike at lag 1 indicates MA(1), and its negative sign means θ is negative. AR(1) would show a decaying ACF and a single PACF spike.

questions.q: For an MA(3) model, what are the forecasts for horizons beyond 3 steps ahead?
options: Equal to the last observed value
Growing linearly with the horizon
Equal to the process mean
Equal to the three-period moving average of recent observations
questions.answer: Equal to the process mean
questions.explanation: Beyond q steps, all shocks in the equation are future ones with zero expectation, so forecasts equal μ. Using a three-period average again confuses MA(q) with smoothing.

questions.q: MA(1) models with θ = 0.5 and θ = 2 produce the same ACF (ρ1 = 0.4). Why do forecasting packages report θ = 0.5?
options: Only θ = 0.5 is invertible, so recent observations get more weight than distant ones and the model is uniquely identified
θ = 2 makes the MA(1) non-stationary, so its variance would keep growing over time and the forecasts would eventually explode
θ = 0.5 always gives a higher R²
θ = 2 implies a unit root that requires differencing
questions.answer: Only θ = 0.5 is invertible, so recent observations get more weight than distant ones and the model is uniquely identified
questions.explanation: Invertibility (|θ| < 1) picks the unique representation in which past observations' influence decays. Both θ values give stationary processes, so non-stationarity is not the reason.

questions.q: A sample lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.4 is observed and an MA(1) is assumed. Solving θ/(1 + θ²) = 0.4 by method of moments, what is the invertible estimate of θ?
questions.explanation: 0.4θ² − θ + 0.4 = 0 gives θ = 0.5 or 2; only 0.5 is invertible. Setting θ = ρ1 = 0.4 skips the equation entirely.

questions.q: A stationary series has sample ACF of 0.7 at lag 1 and nothing significant afterwards. A colleague insists it is MA(1). What is the best response?
options: Accept MA(1), because an ACF that cuts off after lag 1 always identifies an MA(1) regardless of the size of the spike
Fit MA(1) with θ = 0.7
Fit MA(7) to capture the higher correlation
A pure MA(1) cannot have |ρ1| above 0.5, so check sampling error or consider other models such as AR or ARMA
questions.answer: A pure MA(1) cannot have |ρ1| above 0.5, so check sampling error or consider other models such as AR or ARMA
questions.explanation: The MA(1) autocorrelation is bounded at 0.5, so 0.7 is inconsistent with it. Setting θ = 0.7 would imply ρ1 ≈ 0.47, not 0.7.

questions.q: A bank models daily ATM withdrawals as MA(1). A festival causes a large unexpected spike today. How long will this shock influence the model's forecasts?
options: Only tomorrow's forecast; from two days ahead forecasts return to the mean
Permanently, shifting the forecast level
For many days, with the effect decaying geometrically at the rate θ each day
It never affects forecasts because shocks are random
questions.answer: Only tomorrow's forecast; from two days ahead forecasts return to the mean
questions.explanation: An MA(1) remembers exactly one past shock, so its effect lasts one step. Geometric decay describes an AR(1) and permanent shifts describe a unit-root process.

questions.q: Why does the PACF of an invertible MA(1) tail off instead of cutting off?
options: Because MA processes are non-stationary
An invertible MA(1) can be written as an infinite-order AR with geometrically declining weights, so partial correlations persist at all lags
Because the ACF of an MA(1) also tails off, and the PACF always mirrors the shape of the ACF for any stationary moving average process
Because the PACF always tails off for every model
questions.answer: An invertible MA(1) can be written as an infinite-order AR with geometrically declining weights, so partial correlations persist at all lags
questions.explanation: Inverting the MA(1) yields AR(∞), so direct effects exist at every lag and the PACF decays. The ACF of an MA(1) cuts off, so that distractor is false.

questions.q: For an MA(2) with θ1 = 0.5 and θ2 = 0.3, what is ρ2 = θ2/(1 + θ1² + θ2²)?
questions.explanation: ρ2 = 0.3/(1 + 0.25 + 0.09) = 0.3/1.34 ≈ 0.224. Reporting θ2 itself ignores the variance in the denominator; zero would be ρ3.

questions.q: For an MA(2) with θ1 = 0.5 and θ2 = 0.3, what is ρ1 = (θ1 + θ1θ2)/(1 + θ1² + θ2²)?
questions.explanation: ρ1 = (0.5 + 0.15)/1.34 ≈ 0.485. Omitting the θ1θ2 cross term gives 0.5/1.34 ≈ 0.373, and forgetting the denominator gives 0.65.

questions.q: For an MA(2) model, how does the forecast-error variance behave for horizons of 3 steps and beyond?
options: It keeps growing without limit as the horizon increases, as in a random walk
It stays constant at σ²(1 + θ1² + θ2²), the variance of the process
It falls to zero
It oscillates between positive and negative values
questions.answer: It stays constant at σ²(1 + θ1² + θ2²), the variance of the process
questions.explanation: After q steps the forecast is the mean and the error variance equals the unconditional variance, so intervals stop widening. Unbounded growth is a feature of non-stationary (unit-root) models.

questions.q: A firm uses an MA(1) model to forecast quarterly sales eight quarters ahead for capacity planning. What is the main weakness?
options: MA(1) forecasts explode at long horizons, because each forecast feeds the previous forecast error back into the next one
MA(1) cannot produce a one-step forecast
MA(1) forecasts copy the sales from eight quarters ago
Beyond one quarter the forecasts are just the historical mean, so the model gives little information for long-horizon planning
questions.answer: Beyond one quarter the forecasts are just the historical mean, so the model gives little information for long-horizon planning
questions.explanation: An MA(1) forecast reverts to the mean after one step, so long-range capacity decisions get no dynamic signal. It does not explode; that would be a non-stationary model.

questions.q: A stationary demand series is differenced unnecessarily. The differenced series has ACF ≈ −0.5 at lag 1 and nothing after. What has happened?
options: Over-differencing has introduced an MA(1) with θ close to −1, which is near non-invertible
The differenced series is now white noise
A genuine AR(1) structure with φ = −0.5 has been revealed that was hidden in the original levels
The series has acquired a unit root
questions.answer: Over-differencing has introduced an MA(1) with θ close to −1, which is near non-invertible
questions.explanation: Differencing white noise gives ε_t − ε_{t−1}, whose ρ1 = −0.5, an MA(1) with θ = −1. Interpreting it as a real AR(1) misses that the pattern was created by the analyst.

references: A moving average process, MA(q), says today's value equals an average level plus today's random shock plus a weighted share of the last q shocks. A shock is the surprise or forecast error, the part we could not predict. So MA(1) is y_t = μ + ε_t + θε_{t−1}. This is not the same as moving-average smoothing, which averages past sales figures; here we use past errors. Because the model only remembers q shocks, its ACF cuts off after lag q while the PACF tails off. A finite MA is always stationary, and we want it invertible (for MA(1), |θ| < 1). Forecasts beyond q steps simply return to the mean.

Imagine a bank branch where an unexpected rush of withdrawals happens today because of a local festival. Part of that surprise spills into tomorrow, as people who could not be served come back, but after that the effect disappears. That is an MA(1) pattern: tomorrow's forecast is the mean plus θ times today's surprise, and from the second day onward the forecast is just the average. On a correlogram this shows up as one significant ACF spike at lag 1 and nothing after, while the PACF decays gradually. The key point is that the model remembers past errors or shocks, not past sales values, and only for q periods.

For decision-making, an MA(q) model is useful when shocks to the business, such as a promotion, a supply delay or a weather event, have short-lived effects that fade completely after a few periods. It tells managers how much to adjust the next q forecasts after a surprise and reassures them that beyond q periods the forecast reverts to the normal mean level, with a stable forecast-error variance. We identify it when the ACF cuts off after lag q, and we check residuals are white noise. It is a poor choice for long-horizon planning on its own, since it carries no information beyond q periods, and it must not be confused with moving-average smoothing.

questions.q: An autoregressive AR(p) model forecasts y_t using:
options: A linear combination of p past forecast errors plus the current white-noise error
An external explanatory variable lagged p periods
A linear combination of its own p past values plus a white-noise error
The average of the last p observations with equal weights
questions.answer: A linear combination of its own p past values plus a white-noise error
questions.explanation: Autoregressive means the series is regressed on its own lags. Using past forecast errors describes an MA(q) model.

questions.q: Which equation represents an AR(1) process?
options: y_t = μ + ε_t + θε_{t−1}
y_t = c + βt + ε_t
y_t = c + φy_{t−1} + ε_t
questions.answer: y_t = c + φy_{t−1} + ε_t
questions.explanation: AR(1) uses one lagged value of y. μ + ε_t + θε_{t−1} is MA(1) and c + βt is a deterministic trend.

questions.q: An AR(1) process y_t = c + φy_{t−1} + ε_t is stationary when:
options: φ > 0 only
questions.explanation: With |φ| < 1 shocks die out and the mean and variance are constant. φ = 1 gives a unit root (random walk).

questions.q: The theoretical PACF of an AR(p) process:
options: Tails off slowly without cutting off
Cuts off after lag 1 for any p
Cuts off after lag p
Is zero at all lags
questions.answer: Cuts off after lag p
questions.explanation: AR(p) has direct dependence on exactly p lags, so the PACF is zero beyond p. A tailing PACF is the MA signature.

questions.q: The theoretical ACF of a stationary AR(p) process:
options: Cuts off sharply after lag p, exactly mirroring the PACF pattern
Is exactly zero after lag 1
Tails off gradually (exponential decay or damped sine wave)
Stays constant at all lags
questions.answer: Tails off gradually (exponential decay or damped sine wave)
questions.explanation: Because each value depends on earlier values, correlation propagates and the ACF decays. Cutting off after lag p is the ACF behaviour of MA(q).

questions.q: An AR(1) model with c = 0 and φ = 1 is known as a:
options: Random walk
White noise process
Stationary AR(1)
MA(1) process
questions.answer: Random walk
questions.explanation: y_t = y_{t−1} + ε_t is the random walk, which has a unit root and is non-stationary. White noise would need φ = 0.

questions.q: In an AR(p) model, p refers to:
options: The number of times the series is differenced
The number of lagged error terms
The seasonal period
The number of lagged values of the series used as predictors
questions.answer: The number of lagged values of the series used as predictors
questions.explanation: p is the autoregressive order. Lagged errors are counted by q and differences by d.

questions.q: AR models are most natural when:
options: Shocks affect only the current period and vanish immediately
The series is purely random white noise
The series depends only on calendar dates
The current value depends on its own recent past, showing persistence or momentum
questions.answer: The current value depends on its own recent past, showing persistence or momentum
questions.explanation: AR captures persistence: high values tend to follow high values. Shocks vanishing immediately describes white noise.

questions.q: The mean of a stationary AR(1) process y_t = c + φy_{t−1} + ε_t is:
options: c
c/φ
questions.explanation: Setting E(y_t) = E(y_{t−1}) = μ gives μ = c + φμ, so μ = c/(1 − φ). Treating c as the mean is a common error.

questions.q: An AR(1) model with φ = 0 reduces to:
options: White noise around the constant c
A random walk
A deterministic trend
An MA(1) process
questions.answer: White noise around the constant c
questions.explanation: With φ = 0, y_t = c + ε_t, which has no dependence on the past. A random walk needs φ = 1.

questions.q: For the AR(1) model y_t = 20 + 0.6y_{t−1} + ε_t, what is the long-run mean?
questions.explanation: μ = 20/(1 − 0.6) = 50. Taking the constant 20 as the mean ignores the feedback; 33.3 comes from dividing by φ instead of 1 − φ.

questions.q: For y_t = 20 + 0.6y_{t−1} + ε_t, the latest weekly sales are y_T = 60 (₹ lakh). What is the one-step forecast ŷ_{T+1}?
questions.explanation: ŷ_{T+1} = 20 + 0.6 × 60 = 56. Forgetting the constant gives 36; adding 20 to the unweighted last value gives 80.

questions.q: For y_t = 20 + 0.6y_{t−1} + ε_t with y_T = 60, what is the two-step forecast ŷ_{T+2}?
questions.explanation: ŷ_{T+1} = 56, then ŷ_{T+2} = 20 + 0.6 × 56 = 53.6. 50 is the long-run mean reached only as the horizon grows; 33.6 omits the constant.

questions.q: For a stationary AR(1) with φ = 0.8, what is the theoretical autocorrelation at lag 3?
questions.explanation: ρk = φ^k, so ρ3 = 0.8³ = 0.512. Zero at lag 3 is the PACF of an AR(1), and 2.4 multiplies instead of raising to a power.

questions.q: An AR(2) model is y_t = 10 + 0.5y_{t−1} + 0.3y_{t−2} + ε_t. With y_T = 40 and y_{T−1} = 30, what is ŷ_{T+1}?
questions.explanation: ŷ = 10 + 0.5 × 40 + 0.3 × 30 = 39. Swapping the lags (0.5 × 30 + 0.3 × 40 + 10) gives 37, and omitting the constant gives 29.

questions.q: A stationary series has significant PACF spikes at lags 1 and 2 only, while the ACF decays gradually. Which model fits best?
options: MA(2)
AR(2)
AR(1)
ARMA(1,2)
questions.answer: AR(2)
questions.explanation: A PACF cut-off at lag 2 with a tailing ACF identifies AR(2). MA(2) would show the ACF cutting off instead.

questions.q: A hotel's daily booking deviations from target follow an AR(1) with φ = −0.5. What does this imply?
options: Above-target days tend to be followed by more above-target days
An above-target day tends to be followed by a below-target day
Booking deviations are pure white noise
Deviations grow larger over time
questions.answer: An above-target day tends to be followed by a below-target day
questions.explanation: A negative φ produces oscillation: positive deviations are followed by negative ones. Persistence of the same sign requires positive φ.

questions.q: Which AR(1) coefficient gives a stationary process?
questions.explanation: Only |φ| < 1 is stationary, so 0.95 qualifies even though it is highly persistent. φ = 1 is a unit root, and |φ| > 1 is explosive.

questions.q: An AR(1) has φ = 0.8 and error variance σ² = 9. What is Var(y_t) = σ²/(1 − φ²)?
questions.explanation: Var = 9/(1 − 0.64) = 9/0.36 = 25. Using 1 − φ in the denominator gives 45, and ignoring persistence gives 9.

questions.q: In an AR(1) with φ = 0.5, a demand shock of 100 units hits today. How much of the shock remains in the series 3 periods later?
options: 12.5 units
50 units
25 units
0 units
questions.answer: 12.5 units
questions.explanation: The effect after k periods is φ^k × shock = 0.5³ × 100 = 12.5. 50 is the effect after one period and 25 after two.

questions.q: Which AR(2) parameter pair (φ1, φ2) gives a stationary process? (Conditions: φ1 + φ2 < 1, φ2 − φ1 < 1, |φ2| < 1.)
For y_t = 12 + 0.7y_{t−1} + ε_t with the last value y_T = 70, what do forecasts approach as the horizon becomes very long?
options: They grow without limit
questions.explanation: Stationary AR forecasts revert to the mean c/(1 − φ) = 12/0.3 = 40. Staying at 70 is naive-forecast behaviour, typical of a random walk.

questions.q: The ACF of a stationary quarterly demand series shows a damped sine-wave pattern and the PACF has two significant spikes. What is the best interpretation?
options: An AR(2) with complex roots, capturing a pseudo-cyclical pattern
An MA(2), because there are exactly two significant spikes on the correlogram
A random walk with drift
White noise with outliers
questions.answer: An AR(2) with complex roots, capturing a pseudo-cyclical pattern
questions.explanation: AR(2) with φ1² + 4φ2 < 0 has complex roots, producing a damped oscillating ACF, and the PACF cuts off at 2. MA(2) would show two ACF spikes and then zero.

questions.q: Sample autocorrelations are ρ1 = 0.6 and ρ2 = 0.5. Using Yule–Walker for an AR(2), φ2 = (ρ2 − ρ1²)/(1 − ρ1²). What is φ2?
questions.explanation: φ2 = (0.5 − 0.36)/(1 − 0.36) = 0.14/0.64 ≈ 0.219. Stopping at the numerator gives 0.14, and taking ρ2 as φ2 gives 0.5.

questions.q: An FMCG firm estimates an AR(1) for monthly sales and gets φ = 0.99. What is the main implication?
options: Sales revert to their mean within a month
The model is ideal, because a φ close to 1 means past sales explain almost all of the variation in current sales, so no further testing is needed
The series is close to a unit root; shocks persist for a very long time, so test for a unit root and consider differencing
Sales are white noise
questions.answer: The series is close to a unit root; shocks persist for a very long time, so test for a unit root and consider differencing
questions.explanation: φ = 0.99 implies extremely slow mean reversion and is hard to distinguish from a random walk; unit root testing is needed. Fast mean reversion would need a small φ.

questions.q: After fitting an AR(2), the residual ACF has a significant spike at lag 3 and the Ljung–Box p-value is 0.01. What should the analyst do?
options: Accept the model since AR(2) coefficients are significant
Difference the series twice
Drop the AR terms and use the mean as forecast
Revise the model, e.g. try AR(3) or add an MA term, and recheck residuals
questions.answer: Revise the model, e.g. try AR(3) or add an MA term, and recheck residuals
questions.explanation: Remaining residual autocorrelation means the model is under-specified. Significant coefficients do not prove the residuals are white noise.

questions.q: A bank observes that an unexpected jump in deposits fades gradually over several months rather than disappearing after one month. Which model structure fits this behaviour best?
options: MA(1)
White noise
Random walk
AR(1) with a positive φ
questions.answer: AR(1) with a positive φ
questions.explanation: Gradual geometric fading is AR(1) behaviour (effect φ^k). MA(1) would drop the effect after one period and a random walk would make it permanent.

questions.q: For y_t = 10 + 0.8y_{t−1} + ε_t with y_T = 70, what is the two-step forecast ŷ_{T+2}?
questions.explanation: ŷ_{T+1} = 10 + 56 = 66 and ŷ_{T+2} = 10 + 0.8 × 66 = 62.8. 66 is only the one-step forecast; 50 is the long-run mean.

questions.q: For an AR(1) with φ = 0.8, approximately how many periods does it take for a shock to fall to half its initial size (half-life = ln 0.5 / ln φ)?
options: About 2.5 periods
About 3.1 periods
About 0.8 periods
About 5 periods
questions.answer: About 3.1 periods
questions.explanation: ln 0.5 / ln 0.8 = −0.693/−0.223 ≈ 3.1. 2.5 comes from 0.5/(1 − φ) and 5 from 1/(1 − φ), neither of which is the half-life.

questions.q: Why does the ACF of an AR(1) tail off instead of cutting off?
options: Because the AR(1) is non-stationary
Because the error terms in an AR(1) are themselves autocorrelated, so each shock is correlated with all earlier shocks at every lag
Because the ACF of every model tails off
Because y_t depends on y_{t−1}, which depends on y_{t−2}, so every past shock affects y_t with a weight φ^k that decays but never becomes exactly zero
questions.answer: Because y_t depends on y_{t−1}, which depends on y_{t−2}, so every past shock affects y_t with a weight φ^k that decays but never becomes exactly zero
questions.explanation: The AR(1) is equivalent to an MA(∞) with weights φ^k, so correlations decay geometrically. A stationary AR(1) still has a tailing ACF, so non-stationarity is not the reason.

references: An autoregressive model, AR(p), forecasts a series using its own past values. AR(1) is y_t = c + φy_{t−1} + ε_t: this period depends on last period plus a random shock. The order p is how many past values we use. For the model to be stationary, the coefficients must keep shocks from exploding; for AR(1) that means |φ| < 1. If φ = 1 we get a random walk. In an AR process the ACF tails off gradually, while the PACF cuts off after lag p, which is how we identify p. The long-run mean is c/(1 − φ), and forecasts move steadily back toward that mean as the horizon increases.

Consider weekly sales at a supermarket chain. If last week was strong, this week is usually strong too, because of loyal customers and momentum. An AR(1) captures this: forecast = constant + φ × last week's sales. With c = 20 and φ = 0.6, if last week was 60 the forecast is 56, and further forecasts drift toward the long-run mean of 50. A one-off promotion spike fades gradually: with φ = 0.5, half remains after one week, a quarter after two. On the PACF we would see one significant spike at lag 1, and the ACF would decay slowly. If φ were close to 1, the effect would barely fade and the series would behave like a random walk.

For a manager, an AR(p) model is valuable when business performance has persistence: today's demand, deposits or occupancy tell us a lot about tomorrow's. The φ coefficients show how strongly the past carries forward and how quickly shocks die out, which informs inventory buffers and staffing. We choose p by looking at where the PACF cuts off and by comparing AIC, then confirm the residuals are white noise. We must check stationarity: if φ is near 1, shocks are almost permanent, so we should test for a unit root and difference instead. Stationary AR forecasts always revert to a long-run mean, so they suit medium-term planning where things return to normal.

topics.topic: Stationarity and Unit Root Tests (ADF Test)

questions.q: A time series is (weakly) stationary when:
options: Its values never change from one period to the next
Its mean and variance are constant and its autocovariance depends only on the lag
It has a steady upward trend with exactly the same growth in sales in every single period
Its mean is zero but its variance is allowed to grow over time
questions.answer: Its mean and variance are constant and its autocovariance depends only on the lag
questions.explanation: Weak stationarity requires constant mean, constant variance and lag-dependent autocovariance. A steady trend means the mean changes, so a trending series is not stationary.

questions.q: What is the null hypothesis of the Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test?
options: The series has a unit root (it is non-stationary)
The series is stationary (its mean and variance are constant)
The residuals are white noise
The series has no seasonal pattern
questions.answer: The series has a unit root (it is non-stationary)
questions.explanation: ADF's null is a unit root; rejecting it supports stationarity. Assuming the null is stationarity confuses ADF with the KPSS test.

questions.q: If a sales series has a unit root, a one-off shock to sales will:
options: Disappear completely after one period
Fade away geometrically until the series is back at its mean
Have a permanent effect on the level of the series
Affect only the seasonal pattern
questions.answer: Have a permanent effect on the level of the series
questions.explanation: With a unit root, shocks accumulate and permanently shift the level. Geometric fading back to a mean is the behaviour of a stationary AR process.

questions.q: A random walk y_t = y_{t−1} + ε_t is an example of:
options: A stationary series with constant variance
A white noise series
A deterministic linear trend
A non-stationary series with a unit root
questions.answer: A non-stationary series with a unit root
questions.explanation: The random walk has φ = 1, so its variance grows over time. Its differences are white noise, but the level itself is not.

questions.q: An ADF test gives a p-value of 0.01. At the 5% level, the conclusion is:
options: Reject the unit root null; the series can be treated as stationary
Fail to reject the null; the series is non-stationary
Reject stationarity; the series has a unit root and must be differenced first
The test is inconclusive whenever the p-value is below 0.05
questions.answer: Reject the unit root null; the series can be treated as stationary
questions.explanation: p < 0.05 rejects the unit root null, supporting stationarity. Reading a small p-value as 'non-stationary' reverses the ADF hypotheses.

questions.q: ADF in time series analysis stands for:
options: Autoregressive Distributed Forecast
Augmented Dickey–Fuller
Adjusted Durbin–Fisher
Automatic Differencing Function
questions.answer: Augmented Dickey–Fuller
questions.explanation: The ADF test is the Augmented Dickey–Fuller unit root test. Durbin–Watson is a different test for residual autocorrelation.

questions.q: Why is the Dickey–Fuller test 'augmented' in the ADF test?
options: A time trend is always added to every regression
Seasonal dummies are added to remove seasonality
Lagged differences of the series are added to absorb serial correlation in the errors
The sample is augmented with bootstrapped observations to increase the power of the test
questions.answer: Lagged differences of the series are added to absorb serial correlation in the errors
questions.explanation: Adding lagged Δy terms makes the test valid when errors are autocorrelated. A trend term is optional and depends on the data.

questions.q: Which unit root/stationarity test has stationarity as its null hypothesis?
options: ADF test
KPSS test
Dickey–Fuller test
Phillips–Perron test
questions.answer: KPSS test
questions.explanation: KPSS reverses the hypotheses: null = stationary. ADF, Dickey–Fuller and Phillips–Perron all have a unit root as the null.

questions.q: Why do ARMA models require a stationary series?
options: Because stationary series always have zero autocorrelation, which makes ARMA estimation simpler
Because ARMA software cannot read trending data
Because they assume the mean, variance and autocorrelation structure stay stable over time
Because stationary series always produce more accurate forecasts than any other kind of series
questions.answer: Because they assume the mean, variance and autocorrelation structure stay stable over time
questions.explanation: ARMA assumes stable statistical properties so that past patterns describe the future. A stationary series can still be strongly autocorrelated; that is exactly what ARMA models.

questions.q: Which of these series is most likely to be stationary?
options: Daily closing price of a Nifty 50 stock
India's quarterly GDP level
Daily percentage returns of a Nifty 50 stock
Cumulative number of customers of a bank
questions.answer: Daily percentage returns of a Nifty 50 stock
questions.explanation: Returns fluctuate around a stable mean, while prices, GDP levels and cumulative counts trend and wander. Prices are the classic unit-root example.

questions.q: An ADF test on 60 months of a retailer's sales gives a p-value of 0.32. What should the analyst do?
options: Fail to reject the unit root; treat the series as non-stationary and difference it
Reject the unit root because 0.32 is close to zero
Conclude the series is stationary, because a p-value above 0.05 supports the null of stationarity
Conclude that 32% of the variance comes from the trend
questions.answer: Fail to reject the unit root; treat the series as non-stationary and difference it
questions.explanation: p = 0.32 > 0.05 means we cannot reject the unit-root null, so differencing is indicated. Treating a large p-value as evidence of stationarity reverses the logic.

questions.q: The ADF test statistic is −3.8 and the 5% critical value is −2.86. What is the conclusion?
options: Fail to reject the null because −3.8 is smaller than −2.86
Fail to reject the null because the statistic is negative
Reject stationarity; the series has a unit root
Reject the unit root null; the series is stationary
questions.answer: Reject the unit root null; the series is stationary
questions.explanation: ADF is a left-tailed test: a statistic more negative than the critical value rejects the unit root. 'Smaller than the critical value' is exactly the rejection region.

questions.q: The ADF test statistic is −1.9 and the 5% critical value is −2.86. What is the conclusion?
options: Fail to reject the unit root; the series is non-stationary
Reject the unit root because −1.9 is greater than −2.86
Reject the null because the statistic is negative
The series is stationary around a trend
questions.answer: Fail to reject the unit root; the series is non-stationary
questions.explanation: −1.9 is not more negative than −2.86, so it lies outside the left-tail rejection region. Being greater than the critical value means fail to reject.

questions.q: ADF on the levels of a sales series gives p = 0.64; ADF on the first difference gives p = 0.01. What is the order of integration?
options: I(1), so d = 1
I(0), so d = 0
I(2), so d = 2
I(1), so d = 0
questions.answer: I(1), so d = 1
questions.explanation: The level has a unit root and one difference makes it stationary, so it is integrated of order 1. The d in ARIMA equals the order of integration, so 'I(1) with d = 0' is inconsistent.

questions.q: In the ADF regression Δy_t = α + βt + γy_{t−1} + Σδ_iΔy_{t−i} + ε_t, which hypothesis is tested?
options: H0: β = 0 (no trend) against H1: β ≠ 0
H0: γ = 0 (unit root) against H1: γ < 0 (stationary)
H0: α = 0 against H1: α ≠ 0
H0: γ < 0 (stationary) against H1: γ = 0 (unit root)
questions.answer: H0: γ = 0 (unit root) against H1: γ < 0 (stationary)
questions.explanation: The unit-root test is on the coefficient of y_{t−1}; γ = 0 means φ = 1. Testing β only checks for a deterministic trend.

questions.q: A monthly e-commerce sales series shows a clear upward trend. Which ADF specification is most appropriate?
options: Include neither a constant nor a trend in the test regression
Include only seasonal dummies and no constant
Include a quadratic trend and no constant term at all
Include both a constant and a linear trend in the test regression
questions.answer: Include both a constant and a linear trend in the test regression
questions.explanation: When the data trend, the alternative should be trend-stationary, so constant + trend is used. Omitting deterministic terms biases the test toward not rejecting.

questions.q: ADF gives p = 0.45 and KPSS rejects its null at 1%. What do the two tests jointly indicate?
options: Both point to non-stationarity, so the series should be differenced
Both point to stationarity, so no differencing is needed
The tests contradict each other, so the result is meaningless
ADF indicates stationarity while KPSS indicates a unit root
questions.answer: Both point to non-stationarity, so the series should be differenced
questions.explanation: ADF fails to reject a unit root, and KPSS rejects stationarity; both agree the series is non-stationary. Mixing up the two nulls produces the 'contradiction' distractor.

questions.q: An e-commerce firm's monthly GMV grows and its swings get bigger as sales grow. What preparation is most appropriate before ARIMA modelling?
options: Difference only, since differencing also stabilises a growing variance
Take logs to stabilise the variance, then difference to remove the trend
Take logs only, since the log removes the trend as well
Use the raw data, because ARIMA handles changing variance automatically
questions.answer: Take logs to stabilise the variance, then difference to remove the trend
questions.explanation: Logs stabilise multiplicative variance and differencing removes the stochastic trend; each solves a different problem. Differencing alone does not fix growing variance.

questions.q: For y_t = 2 + y_{t−1} + ε_t (a random walk with drift), the first difference Δy_t is:
options: White noise with mean 0
A random walk without drift
White noise with mean 2
An AR(1) with φ = 2
questions.answer: White noise with mean 2
questions.explanation: Δy_t = 2 + ε_t, which is stationary with mean 2 (the drift). Dropping the constant gives mean 0, which ignores the drift.

questions.q: An ADF test gives p = 0.06 and the analyst uses a 5% significance level. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: Reject the unit root at 5%, because 0.06 is close enough to 0.05 to count as significant evidence
Conclude the series is definitely stationary
Conclude the series is I(2) and must be differenced twice
Fail to reject the unit root at 5%; the evidence is borderline, so check KPSS and the plots
questions.answer: Fail to reject the unit root at 5%; the evidence is borderline, so check KPSS and the plots
questions.explanation: 0.06 > 0.05 means we fail to reject at 5%, but borderline evidence calls for supporting checks. Rounding the p-value down to 'significant' is a common error.

questions.q: Why are ordinary t-table critical values not used for the ADF test statistic?
options: Because the ADF statistic is always positive and so needs one-sided values from the F-table instead
Because the t-distribution only applies to samples smaller than 30
Under the unit-root null the statistic follows a non-standard Dickey–Fuller distribution with more negative critical values
Because the ADF test uses a chi-square statistic
questions.answer: Under the unit-root null the statistic follows a non-standard Dickey–Fuller distribution with more negative critical values
questions.explanation: Under non-stationarity, standard asymptotics fail, so Dickey–Fuller tabulated values (e.g. −2.86 at 5% with a constant) are used. Using −1.65 would over-reject the unit root.

questions.q: A hotel chain's revenue follows y_t = a + bt + u_t where u_t is stationary. What is the right treatment and what does it imply about shocks?
options: Detrend the series (it is trend-stationary); shocks are temporary and revenue returns to the trend line
Difference the series (it has a unit root); shocks permanently shift revenue away from the trend
No treatment is needed because the deviations u_t are stationary
Take logs only; shocks then become permanent shifts in the level
questions.answer: Detrend the series (it is trend-stationary); shocks are temporary and revenue returns to the trend line
questions.explanation: A deterministic trend with stationary deviations is trend-stationary: shocks die out. Differencing it would over-difference and add a non-invertible MA term.

questions.q: A retailer's sales have a unit root. What does this imply for long-horizon forecasts?
options: Prediction intervals keep widening as the horizon grows, because shocks accumulate permanently
Prediction intervals stay constant at all horizons
Forecasts revert quickly to the historical mean
Prediction intervals shrink, since a longer horizon averages out more of the shocks over the long run
questions.answer: Prediction intervals keep widening as the horizon grows, because shocks accumulate permanently
questions.explanation: Under a unit root, forecast-error variance grows with the horizon, so intervals fan out. Constant intervals and mean reversion are features of stationary series.

questions.q: How should the number of lagged differences in an ADF regression be chosen?
options: Always use exactly one lag regardless of data frequency
Using an information criterion (AIC/BIC) or by checking that test residuals are free of autocorrelation
Use as many lags as there are observations divided by two
Choose the number of lags that gives the most negative test statistic so that the unit root is rejected
questions.answer: Using an information criterion (AIC/BIC) or by checking that test residuals are free of autocorrelation
questions.explanation: Too few lags leave autocorrelation and distort the test size; too many reduce power, so criteria such as AIC/BIC are used. Picking lags to force rejection is data snooping.

questions.q: With only 30 observations of a series that has φ ≈ 0.95, the ADF test fails to reject the unit root. What is the best interpretation?
options: The series definitely has a unit root, because the ADF test did not reject its null hypothesis of non-stationarity
The series is definitely stationary because φ is below 1
ADF has low power near a unit root in small samples, so failing to reject is not proof of a unit root
The test proves the series is white noise because it is short
questions.answer: ADF has low power near a unit root in small samples, so failing to reject is not proof of a unit root
questions.explanation: Failure to reject is weak evidence, especially with near-unit-root, short samples; complementary KPSS and judgement help. 'Fail to reject' never proves the null.

questions.q: An FMCG sales series has a sharp level shift at the 2017 GST rollout. Standard ADF fails to reject the unit root. What is a key concern?
options: Structural breaks make ADF reject too often, so the series is truly stationary
A structural break can make a stationary series look like it has a unit root; use a break-robust test such as Zivot–Andrews
ADF automatically adjusts for any structural break
A structural break proves the series has a unit root, so the series should be differenced twice before any ARIMA modelling begins
questions.answer: A structural break can make a stationary series look like it has a unit root; use a break-robust test such as Zivot–Andrews
questions.explanation: Unmodelled breaks bias ADF toward non-rejection. Break-robust tests or intervention dummies separate a one-time shift from a genuine unit root.

questions.q: A regression of a retailer's sales level on India's GDP level (both I(1)) gives R² = 0.97. What is the main risk?
options: None, since an R² of 0.97 together with significant t-statistics proves a strong causal relationship between the two series
Multicollinearity, because there is only one regressor
Heteroskedasticity, which is the only problem with time series regressions
Spurious regression: two unrelated trending series can show a high R², so test for cointegration or model differences
questions.answer: Spurious regression: two unrelated trending series can show a high R², so test for cointegration or model differences
questions.explanation: Regressing one non-stationary series on another often yields high R² and significant t-statistics even without a true relationship. High R² is not evidence of causation.

questions.q: ADF p-values are 0.80 for the levels, 0.45 for the first difference and 0.001 for the second difference. What is the order of integration?
options: I(1), so d = 1
I(0), so d = 0
I(3), so d = 3
I(2), so d = 2
questions.answer: I(2), so d = 2
questions.explanation: Stationarity is achieved only after two differences, so the series is I(2). Stopping at d = 1 ignores that the first difference still has a unit root.

questions.q: In an ADF test with constant and trend, the statistic is −3.10. Critical values are −3.96 (1%), −3.41 (5%) and −3.13 (10%). What is the conclusion?
options: Reject the unit root at 10% but not at 5%
Reject the unit root at 5%
Reject the unit root at 1%
Fail to reject the unit root even at the 10% level
questions.answer: Fail to reject the unit root even at the 10% level
questions.explanation: −3.10 is less negative than −3.13, so it does not reach even the 10% critical value. Many students wrongly round −3.10 as 'about −3.13' and reject.

questions.q: A demand series has constant mean and variance, but its lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.6 in the first half and 0.1 in the second half. Is it weakly stationary?
options: Yes, because the mean and variance are constant
No, because the autocovariance structure changes over time
Yes, because autocorrelation does not affect stationarity
No, because any lag-1 autocorrelation above 0.5 is non-stationary
questions.answer: No, because the autocovariance structure changes over time
questions.explanation: Weak stationarity also requires autocovariances to depend only on lag, not on time. A large but stable autocorrelation would be perfectly compatible with stationarity.

references: A series is stationary when its statistical behaviour does not change over time: the mean and variance stay constant and the correlation between periods depends only on how far apart they are. Most sales series with trends are not stationary. A unit root is a type of non-stationarity where shocks have permanent effects, as in a random walk. The Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test checks for this. Its null hypothesis is that the series has a unit root, i.e. is non-stationary. If the p-value is below 0.05, or the test statistic is more negative than the critical value, we reject the null and treat the series as stationary. If not, we difference the series and test again.

Compare a share's daily price with its daily return. The price wanders: a big fall today shifts all future prices, so it has a unit root and is non-stationary. The return bounces around a stable average, so it is stationary. Before building an ARIMA model for, say, a retailer's monthly sales, I run the ADF test. Suppose the p-value is 0.40: we cannot reject the null of a unit root, so I take the first difference. If the ADF on the differenced data gives p = 0.01, the differenced series is stationary and d = 1. I often confirm with the KPSS test, whose null is the opposite, that the series is stationary.

Stationarity matters to managers because models like ARMA assume the past behaves like the future. If sales have a unit root, shocks such as a lost distributor permanently change the level, forecasts carry no pull back to an average, and prediction intervals widen with the horizon. The ADF test decides how to prepare the data: a high p-value means we fail to reject non-stationarity and should difference; a low p-value means the series is stationary and can be modelled directly. We should not over-trust the test: it has low power in short samples and can be fooled by structural breaks like GST or COVID, so plots, KPSS and business judgement should support the decision.

questions.q: The first difference of a series y_t is defined as:
questions.explanation: First differencing subtracts the previous value. y_t − y_{t−12} is a seasonal difference for monthly data.

questions.q: Using the backshift (lag) operator B, the expression By_t equals:
options: B × y_t as an ordinary multiplication
questions.explanation: B shifts the series back one period: By_t = y_{t−1}. The difference y_t − y_{t−1} is (1 − B)y_t, not By_t.

questions.q: For monthly data, the seasonal difference of y_t is:
questions.explanation: A seasonal difference subtracts the value from the same season one year earlier, which is 12 months back. y_t − y_{t−4} would be for quarterly data.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of differencing a time series?
options: To remove trend and stabilise the mean so that the series becomes stationary
To stabilise a variance that grows with the level of the series
To remove random noise so the series looks smooth
To increase the number of observations available for modelling
questions.answer: To remove trend and stabilise the mean so that the series becomes stationary
questions.explanation: Differencing removes changes in level (trend) and helps achieve a stable mean. Stabilising a growing variance is the job of a log or Box–Cox transformation.

questions.q: A series has 48 observations. How many values does the first-differenced series have?
questions.explanation: Each difference needs a previous value, so the first observation has no difference and one value is lost. Two would be lost after second differencing.

questions.q: The second difference Δ²y_t equals:
questions.explanation: Δ²y_t = Δy_t − Δy_{t−1} = y_t − 2y_{t−1} + y_{t−2}. y_t − y_{t−2} is a lag-2 difference, not a second difference.

questions.q: The lag-k value of a series at time t refers to:
options: The value expected k periods later, y_{t+k}
The average of the last k values of the series
The value observed k periods earlier, y_{t−k}
The change in the series over the last k periods
questions.answer: The value observed k periods earlier, y_{t−k}
questions.explanation: A lag looks back k periods. Looking forward would be a lead, and averaging k values is smoothing.

questions.q: In ARIMA(p,d,q), the number of ordinary differences applied is given by:
options: d
p
q
s
questions.answer: d
questions.explanation: d counts differences; p and q are the AR and MA orders and s is the seasonal period in SARIMA.

questions.q: Which transformation is used to stabilise a variance that increases with the level of sales?
options: Taking logarithms
Taking the first difference
Taking a seasonal difference
Adding a lagged value
questions.answer: Taking logarithms
questions.explanation: Logs turn multiplicative changes into additive ones and stabilise variance. Differencing stabilises the mean, not the variance.

questions.q: For quarterly data, the seasonal difference uses a lag of:
questions.explanation: There are four quarters in a year, so the seasonal lag is 4. Lag 12 is for monthly data and lag 7 for daily data with a weekly cycle.

questions.q: Quarterly sales of a two-wheeler dealer are 100, 104, 110, 113. What are the first differences?
questions.explanation: Differences are 104 − 100 = 4, 110 − 104 = 6, 113 − 110 = 3. 4, 10, 13 measures change from the first value, and 2, −3 are the second differences.

questions.q: For the sales series 100, 104, 110, 113, what are the second differences?
questions.explanation: First differences are 4, 6, 3; differencing again gives 6 − 4 = 2 and 3 − 6 = −3. 6, 9 and 10, 9 are lag-2 changes of the original series, not second differences.

questions.q: A retailer's sales were ₹500 lakh in January 2025, ₹520 lakh in December 2024 and ₹450 lakh in January 2024. What is the seasonal (lag-12) difference for January 2025?
questions.explanation: Seasonal difference = Jan 2025 − Jan 2024 = 500 − 450 = 50. −20 is the ordinary first difference (500 − 520).

questions.q: Using the backshift operator, (1 − B)²y_t equals:
options: y_t − y_{t−1}²
questions.explanation: (1 − B)² = 1 − 2B + B², which applied to y_t gives the second difference. y_t − y_{t−2} is (1 − B²)y_t, a different operation.

questions.q: A model forecasts the first difference of daily orders as Δŷ_{T+1} = 8 and Δŷ_{T+2} = 5. The last actual value is y_T = 250. What is ŷ_{T+2}?
questions.explanation: ŷ_{T+1} = 250 + 8 = 258 and ŷ_{T+2} = 258 + 5 = 263. 255 adds only the second difference to y_T; 13 forgets to add back the level.

questions.q: A series grows by roughly the same absolute amount every period (a linear trend with noise). How many ordinary differences are usually needed?
questions.explanation: One difference turns a linear trend into a constant mean. Two differences are needed for curvature (e.g. a quadratic trend).

questions.q: Monthly sales rise from 100 to 110. What is the log difference ln(110) − ln(100), and how is it interpreted?
options: Exactly 10, the absolute increase in sales
About 0.010, approximately a 1% growth rate
About 0.095, approximately a 9.5% growth rate
About 1.100, approximately a 110% growth rate
questions.answer: About 0.095, approximately a 9.5% growth rate
questions.explanation: ln(1.1) ≈ 0.0953, which approximates the percentage change. 1.1 is the ratio, not the log difference.

questions.q: You create a lag-1 column for 24 months of sales data to use as a predictor. How many complete rows (with both y_t and y_{t−1}) are available?
questions.explanation: The first month has no previous value, so one row is lost. 22 would be the count for a lag-2 column.

questions.q: Applying both a seasonal (lag-12) and a first difference, (1 − B)(1 − B¹²)y_t equals:
questions.explanation: (1 − B)(1 − B¹²) = 1 − B − B¹² + B¹³. Missing the + y_{t−13} cross term is the most common error.

questions.q: A monthly series has 60 observations. After one seasonal difference (lag 12) and one first difference, how many observations remain?
questions.explanation: The seasonal difference loses 12 (leaving 48) and the first difference loses 1 more, giving 47. 48 forgets the first difference.

questions.q: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos recommend applying the seasonal difference first when data are strongly seasonal. Why?
options: Because the order of differencing changes the final differenced values
Because first differencing removes all seasonality automatically
The seasonally differenced series may already be stationary, avoiding an unnecessary first difference
Because seasonal differencing first preserves the original level, so the forecasts do not need to be undifferenced
questions.answer: The seasonally differenced series may already be stationary, avoiding an unnecessary first difference
questions.explanation: Seasonal and first differencing commute, so the result is the same either way; doing the seasonal one first lets you check whether a further difference is needed. The claim that order changes the result is false.

questions.q: A demand series has standard deviation 12 in levels, 5 after one difference and 8 after two differences. Which d is suggested?
questions.explanation: The variance falls after the first difference and rises after the second, a sign that the second difference is over-differencing. Choosing d = 2 adds noise and a non-invertible MA component.

questions.q: A model is fitted to second differences. y_T = 200, y_{T−1} = 190 and the forecast second difference is Δ²ŷ_{T+1} = 2. What is ŷ_{T+1}?
questions.explanation: Last first difference = 10, so Δŷ_{T+1} = 10 + 2 = 12 and ŷ_{T+1} = 200 + 12 = 212. 202 adds the second difference directly to the level, skipping one integration step.

questions.q: A SARIMA model forecasts the seasonal difference for December 2026 as +30. December 2025 sales were 820 and November 2026 sales were 790. What is the December 2026 forecast?
questions.explanation: y_{Dec 2026} = y_{Dec 2025} + 30 = 850. Adding the seasonal difference to November 2026 (820) mixes a lag-12 difference with a lag-1 level.

questions.q: A planner objects that a model built on differenced data 'throws away the level', so its forecasts will be wrong. What is the correct response?
options: The planner is right: differenced models can only forecast changes, never levels
The level is restored by adding the series mean to each forecast difference
Forecasts of the differences are added back cumulatively to the last observed level, so the level is restored
Differencing keeps the level, so forecasts of differences are themselves the sales forecasts
questions.answer: Forecasts of the differences are added back cumulatively to the last observed level, so the level is restored
questions.explanation: Integration (cumulative summing from the last actual) reconstructs level forecasts. Adding the overall mean ignores where the series currently is.

questions.q: Sales follow y_t = 50 + 3t + ε_t, where ε_t is white noise. What does the first difference Δy_t equal?
options: 3 + ε_t, which is white noise with mean 3
3 + ε_t − ε_{t−1}, an MA(1) with θ = −1 that is non-invertible
3t + ε_t, a series with a smaller trend
ε_t − ε_{t−1}, which is white noise with mean 0
questions.answer: 3 + ε_t − ε_{t−1}, an MA(1) with θ = −1 that is non-invertible
questions.explanation: Differencing a trend-stationary series removes the trend but leaves ε_t − ε_{t−1}, a non-invertible MA(1). Forgetting the lagged error gives the white-noise distractor.

questions.q: Expand the model (1 − 0.6B)(1 − B)y_t = ε_t into an equation for y_t.
questions.explanation: (1 − 0.6B)(1 − B) = 1 − 1.6B + 0.6B², so y_t = 1.6y_{t−1} − 0.6y_{t−2} + ε_t. Getting the sign of the B² term wrong is the usual slip.

questions.q: A grocery delivery app builds a regression to forecast daily orders using lagged values as predictors. Which set of lags is most sensible to start with?
options: Lags 1 and 7, capturing yesterday's level and the same weekday last week
Lags 1 and 12, capturing yesterday's level and the same month last year
Lags 1 to 365, so that no possible pattern is missed
Only lag 30, because monthly patterns dominate daily data
questions.answer: Lags 1 and 7, capturing yesterday's level and the same weekday last week
questions.explanation: Daily retail demand typically has short-run persistence and a weekly cycle, so lags 1 and 7 are natural. Lag 12 is the seasonal lag for monthly, not daily, data.

questions.q: A year of daily sales (365 observations) is seasonally differenced at lag 7 and then first differenced. How many observations remain?
questions.explanation: The lag-7 difference loses 7 (358 remain), then the first difference loses 1 more, leaving 357. 358 forgets the first difference.

questions.q: Why do prediction intervals from a model with d = 1 keep widening as the forecast horizon increases?
options: Because differencing makes the residuals non-normal at longer horizons
Because the model is re-estimated with fewer observations at each horizon
Because the differenced series has a larger mean than the original series
Forecast errors of the differences accumulate when they are summed back into levels
questions.answer: Forecast errors of the differences accumulate when they are summed back into levels
questions.explanation: Each level forecast is the sum of forecast differences, so error variances add up over the horizon. Stationary (d = 0) models instead have intervals that level off.

references: Differencing means replacing each value with its change from an earlier value. The first difference is y_t − y_{t−1}, the change from last period. We do this to remove a trend and make the mean constant so the series is stationary, which ARIMA models require. If one difference is not enough, a second difference can be taken. A seasonal difference, y_t − y_{t−12} for monthly data, removes a repeating yearly pattern. A lag simply means an earlier value: lag 1 is last period, lag 12 is the same month last year. The backshift operator B writes this compactly, so By_t = y_{t−1}. Each difference loses observations, and logs, not differencing, are used to stabilise variance.

Suppose a dealer's quarterly sales are 100, 104, 110 and 113. The level keeps rising, but the first differences, 4, 6 and 3, hover around a stable value. That differenced series is what the ARIMA model is fitted to. For a retailer with strong festive peaks, I would compare January this year with January last year, a seasonal difference at lag 12, to strip out the annual pattern. To get back to sales levels, the forecast changes are added to the last actual value: if sales were 250 and the model predicts increases of 8 and 5, forecasts are 258 and 263. Lags are also used as predictors, such as yesterday's and last week's orders.

For managers, differencing is the step that turns a drifting, trending sales series into something a forecasting model can learn from. The decision is how many differences to take: usually one, sometimes a seasonal difference as well, and rarely more, because over-differencing adds noise and increases forecast error. We decide using ADF or KPSS tests, the ACF plot and whether variance falls after differencing. Choosing the right lags matters too: lag 1 captures momentum and the seasonal lag, such as 7 for daily or 12 for monthly data, captures repeating cycles. Because differenced forecasts are summed back into levels, uncertainty grows with the horizon, which should be reflected in safety stock and budget ranges.

questions.q: An ARMA(p,q) model combines:
options: p lagged errors and q lagged values of the series
p differences and q seasonal terms
A trend component and a seasonal component estimated by smoothing
p autoregressive terms (lagged values) and q moving-average terms (lagged errors)
questions.answer: p autoregressive terms (lagged values) and q moving-average terms (lagged errors)
questions.explanation: ARMA = AR part on past values + MA part on past shocks. Swapping p and q, or confusing ARMA with decomposition, are common errors.

questions.q: Which equation represents an ARMA(1,1) process?
options: y_t = c + φy_{t−1} + ε_t
y_t = μ + ε_t + θε_{t−1}
y_t = c + φy_{t−1} + ε_t + θε_{t−1}
questions.answer: y_t = c + φy_{t−1} + ε_t + θε_{t−1}
questions.explanation: ARMA(1,1) has one lagged value and one lagged error. y_t = y_{t−1} + ε_t + θε_{t−1} is ARIMA(0,1,1), which includes a difference.

questions.q: ARMA models are applied directly to series that are:
options: Stationary
Trending upward
