Explosive
Seasonal with a changing level
questions.answer: Stationary
questions.explanation: ARMA assumes constant mean and variance; trending series must first be differenced (giving ARIMA). Seasonal series with changing levels need seasonal treatment.

questions.q: For a mixed ARMA(p,q) process, the theoretical ACF and PACF:
options: Both cut off sharply
ACF cuts off and PACF tails off
PACF cuts off and ACF tails off
Both tail off gradually
questions.answer: Both tail off gradually
questions.explanation: With both AR and MA components, neither function has a clean cut-off. ACF cutting off is the MA signature; PACF cutting off is the AR signature.

questions.q: An ARMA(p,0) model is the same as:
options: AR(p)
MA(p)
White noise
ARIMA(0,p,0)
questions.answer: AR(p)
questions.explanation: With q = 0 there are no MA terms, leaving a pure AR(p). ARIMA(0,p,0) would mean differencing p times.

questions.q: An ARMA(0,q) model is the same as:
options: AR(q)
ARIMA(q,0,0)
MA(q)
A random walk
questions.answer: MA(q)
questions.explanation: With p = 0 there are no AR terms, leaving MA(q). ARIMA(q,0,0) is an AR(q).

questions.q: A key advantage of ARMA models over pure AR or pure MA models is:
options: They never require the series to be stationary
Parsimony: they can describe complex autocorrelation with fewer parameters
They always give perfect in-sample fit
They automatically model seasonality and trend without any extra terms
questions.answer: Parsimony: they can describe complex autocorrelation with fewer parameters
questions.explanation: A low-order ARMA such as ARMA(1,1) can mimic a high-order pure AR or MA. ARMA still requires stationarity.

questions.q: When comparing candidate ARMA models fitted to the same data, the model with the ___ AIC is preferred.
options: Highest
Lowest
Closest to zero in absolute value
Closest to 1
questions.answer: Lowest
questions.explanation: AIC balances fit and complexity; lower is better. AIC values can be negative, so 'closest to zero' is not the rule.

questions.q: In an ARMA model, stationarity depends on the ___ part and invertibility depends on the ___ part.
options: MA; AR
AR; AR
AR; MA
MA; MA
questions.answer: AR; MA
questions.explanation: Stationarity is governed by the AR coefficients and invertibility by the MA coefficients. Swapping them is a common slip.

questions.q: An ARMA(p,q) model is the same as:
options: ARIMA(p,1,q)
ARIMA(p,0,q)
ARIMA(0,p,q)
questions.answer: ARIMA(p,0,q)
questions.explanation: ARMA is ARIMA with d = 0, i.e. no differencing. ARIMA(p,1,q) applies ARMA to first differences.

questions.q: An ARMA(1,1) for weekly demand is y_t = 10 + 0.5y_{t−1} + ε_t + 0.4ε_{t−1}. With y_T = 30 and ε_T = 5, what is ŷ_{T+1}?
questions.explanation: ŷ = 10 + 0.5 × 30 + 0.4 × 5 = 27. Dropping the MA term gives 25, and forgetting the constant gives 17.
Two steps ahead the MA term involves a future shock (expected 0), so ŷ_{T+2} = 10 + 0.5 × 27 = 23.5. 25.5 wrongly adds 0.4 × 5 again; 20 is the long-run mean.

questions.q: Three models fitted to the same stationary series have AIC values: AR(2) = 512.4, MA(2) = 515.1, ARMA(1,1) = 508.7. Which is preferred?
options: ARMA(1,1)
MA(2)
AR(2)
None, because AIC values above 500 indicate a poor fit
questions.answer: ARMA(1,1)
questions.explanation: The lowest AIC (508.7) wins. AIC is relative, so its absolute size says nothing about fit quality.

questions.q: Including the constant but excluding the error variance, how many coefficients does an ARMA(2,1) model estimate?
questions.explanation: φ1, φ2, θ1 and c make 4. Counting σ² as well gives 5; forgetting the constant gives 3.

questions.q: After fitting an ARMA(1,1) to daily call-centre volume, the Ljung–Box p-value on residuals is 0.65. What does this suggest?
options: Significant residual autocorrelation remains, so more terms are needed
The model explains 65% of the variation
The original series has a unit root and must be differenced
The residuals behave like white noise, so the model is adequate
questions.answer: The residuals behave like white noise, so the model is adequate
questions.explanation: A large p-value means no evidence of residual autocorrelation. Interpreting p as variance explained is incorrect.

questions.q: What is the long-run mean of y_t = 10 + 0.5y_{t−1} + ε_t + 0.4ε_{t−1}?
questions.explanation: The mean depends only on the AR part: μ = c/(1 − φ) = 10/0.5 = 20. Including θ (e.g. 10/(1 − 0.5 + 0.1)) gives 16.7, but MA terms do not affect the mean.

questions.q: A bank's stationary daily call volume shows an ACF tailing off from lag 1 and a PACF also tailing off from lag 1. Which candidate should lead the shortlist?
options: ARMA(1,1)
AR(1)
MA(1)
White noise
questions.answer: ARMA(1,1)
questions.explanation: When both ACF and PACF decay, a mixed ARMA is indicated, and ARMA(1,1) is the simplest such model. Pure AR(1) would show a PACF cut-off.

questions.q: An analyst estimates an ARMA(1,1) with φ = 1.1 and θ = 0.3. What is wrong?
options: The MA coefficient θ = 0.3 makes the model non-invertible
The AR coefficient exceeds 1 in absolute value, so the process is non-stationary (explosive)
Nothing is wrong, since φ and θ add up to 1.4, which is fine
θ must always be larger than φ in an ARMA model
questions.answer: The AR coefficient exceeds 1 in absolute value, so the process is non-stationary (explosive)
questions.explanation: Stationarity requires |φ| < 1; φ = 1.1 implies explosive behaviour. θ = 0.3 satisfies invertibility (|θ| < 1).

questions.q: Beyond the first step, how do forecasts from a stationary ARMA(1,1) behave?
options: They decay geometrically toward the mean at rate φ, because the MA term only affects the first step
They stay constant at the last observed value forever
They grow linearly at a rate equal to θ, because the MA term adds to each step
They oscillate with increasing amplitude
questions.answer: They decay geometrically toward the mean at rate φ, because the MA term only affects the first step
questions.explanation: After one step the MA(1) contribution is zero, so forecasts follow the AR(1) recursion toward the mean. Staying at the last value is random-walk behaviour.

questions.q: Why does BIC tend to select smaller ARMA models than AIC?
options: BIC penalises each extra parameter by ln(n) rather than 2, a heavier penalty for typical sample sizes
BIC ignores the likelihood and counts only the number of parameters
AIC penalises extra parameters more heavily than BIC does
BIC is computed only on the test set while AIC uses the training set
questions.answer: BIC penalises each extra parameter by ln(n) rather than 2, a heavier penalty for typical sample sizes
questions.explanation: For n > 7, ln(n) > 2, so BIC's penalty per parameter is larger. Both criteria use the likelihood plus a penalty.

questions.q: An ARMA(1,1) is estimated as (1 − 0.5B)y_t = (1 − 0.5B)ε_t. What does this imply?
options: The series is a strongly persistent AR(1) process
The AR and MA factors cancel, so the series is really white noise and the model is over-parameterised
The model is optimal because both coefficients are equal
The series has a unit root that both terms are trying to capture
questions.answer: The AR and MA factors cancel, so the series is really white noise and the model is over-parameterised
questions.explanation: Common factors cancel, leaving y_t = ε_t; the parameters are not identified. Near-cancelling φ and θ is a classic warning sign of over-fitting.

questions.q: For a stationary ARMA(1,1) with φ = 0.5, the lag-1 autocorrelation is ρ1 ≈ 0.69. What is ρ2?
questions.explanation: For ARMA(1,1), ρk = φρ_{k−1} for k ≥ 2, so ρ2 = 0.5 × 0.69 ≈ 0.35. Zero would apply to a pure MA(1); 0.48 squares ρ1 as if it were AR(1) with φ = ρ1.

questions.q: Model A has log-likelihood −250 with 3 parameters; Model B has log-likelihood −247 with 5 parameters. Using AIC = −2logL + 2k, which is preferred?
options: Model A (AIC 506 vs 504)
Model A, because fewer parameters always win
Model B (AIC 504 vs 506)
Model B (AIC 494 vs 500)
questions.answer: Model B (AIC 504 vs 506)
questions.explanation: AIC_A = 500 + 6 = 506 and AIC_B = 494 + 10 = 504, so B wins narrowly. Forgetting the penalty term gives 500 vs 494.

questions.q: ARMA(3,3) has a slightly lower AIC than ARMA(1,1) on training data, but a clearly higher RMSE on a 12-month holdout. Which should a planning manager adopt?
options: ARMA(3,3), because a lower AIC on training data always means better forecasts
Both, by averaging them regardless of their accuracy on the holdout
ARMA(1,1), because it forecasts better out of sample and is more parsimonious
Neither, because both models must be wrong if they disagree
questions.answer: ARMA(1,1), because it forecasts better out of sample and is more parsimonious
questions.explanation: Holdout accuracy is the most direct evidence of forecasting value, and the simpler model is less likely to over-fit. AIC is a proxy, not a guarantee.

questions.q: What justifies using low-order ARMA models for a wide range of stationary business series?
options: All business series are exactly ARMA(1,1) processes by definition
ARMA models can perfectly fit any trending or seasonal series without differencing
Any stationary series can be written as an MA(∞) (Wold), and ARMA gives a parsimonious approximation to that infinite structure
Low-order ARMA models are justified because they can never over-fit a series
questions.answer: Any stationary series can be written as an MA(∞) (Wold), and ARMA gives a parsimonious approximation to that infinite structure
questions.explanation: Wold's theorem supports approximating stationary dynamics with a rational ARMA form. ARMA still needs stationarity, and it can over-fit.

questions.q: Since ACF and PACF both tail off for ARMA, how are p and q typically chosen in practice?
options: Fit a grid of candidate orders and compare AIC/AICc/BIC, then check the residuals (as auto.arima does)
Set p equal to q equal to the number of significant ACF lags
Always use ARMA(1,1) because higher orders cannot be estimated
Choose the orders that maximise in-sample R², since a higher R² always means a better ARMA model
questions.answer: Fit a grid of candidate orders and compare AIC/AICc/BIC, then check the residuals (as auto.arima does)
questions.explanation: Because cut-offs are not visible, a search over orders with information criteria plus residual diagnostics is standard. Maximising in-sample R² favours over-fitting.

questions.q: Which AR(2) part makes an ARMA(2,1) stationary? (Conditions: φ1 + φ2 < 1, φ2 − φ1 < 1, |φ2| < 1.)
ARMA(1,1): y_t = 10 + 0.5y_{t−1} + ε_t + 0.4ε_{t−1}, y_T = 30, ε_T = 5. What is the three-step forecast ŷ_{T+3}?
questions.explanation: ŷ_{T+1} = 27, ŷ_{T+2} = 23.5, ŷ_{T+3} = 10 + 0.5 × 23.5 = 21.75, converging to the mean of 20. 23.75 wrongly adds the MA term 0.4 × 5 again.

questions.q: After fitting ARMA(1,1) to stationary daily sales of a quick-commerce store, the residual ACF has significant spikes at lags 7 and 14. What should be done?
options: Increase to ARMA(14,14) to cover all lags up to 14
Add seasonal (weekly, s = 7) terms, e.g. move to a seasonal ARMA/SARIMA model
Accept the model since the main lags 1 and 2 are clean
Difference the series twice to remove the spikes
questions.answer: Add seasonal (weekly, s = 7) terms, e.g. move to a seasonal ARMA/SARIMA model
questions.explanation: Spikes at multiples of 7 reveal weekly seasonality that ARMA(1,1) ignores; a seasonal term handles it parsimoniously. ARMA(14,14) wastes many parameters.

questions.q: An analyst fits ARMA(1,1) to the raw level of a fast-growing e-commerce GMV series and gets φ = 0.995. What is the best response?
options: Accept the model since φ < 1 proves stationarity
Increase p until φ falls below 0.9
Remove the MA term and refit it as a pure AR(1) on the same raw levels of GMV
Test for a unit root and difference the series, i.e. move to an ARIMA model
questions.answer: Test for a unit root and difference the series, i.e. move to an ARIMA model
questions.explanation: φ ≈ 1 on trending data signals a unit root; ARMA forecasts would wrongly pull GMV back to a historical mean. Differencing (ARIMA) is the appropriate fix.

references: An ARMA(p,q) model combines two ideas. The autoregressive part uses p past values of the series, capturing persistence, and the moving-average part uses q past forecast errors, capturing how recent surprises carry over. ARMA(1,1) is y_t = c + φy_{t−1} + ε_t + θε_{t−1}. It is applied to stationary data; if the series trends, we difference first, which turns it into ARIMA. The AR coefficients must satisfy stationarity and the MA coefficients invertibility. For a mixed ARMA, both the ACF and PACF tail off rather than cutting off, so we usually choose p and q by comparing AIC or BIC across candidates and then check the residuals are white noise.

Take daily call volumes at a bank's call centre, which are stable over time. Busy days tend to follow busy days (the AR part), and an unexpected spike, like an app outage, spills into the next day as customers call back (the MA part). An ARMA(1,1) handles both with just two coefficients. With y_t = 10 + 0.5y_{t−1} + ε_t + 0.4ε_{t−1}, if today was 30 with a surprise of 5, tomorrow's forecast is 10 + 15 + 2 = 27. After that, the surprise no longer matters and forecasts drift back toward the average of 20. A pure AR or MA might need many more terms to match this behaviour.

From a manager's perspective, ARMA is a compact, efficient way to forecast a stable, stationary business metric when both momentum and short-lived shocks matter. Its value is parsimony: fewer parameters mean less over-fitting and more reliable forecasts. The practical workflow is to confirm stationarity, try a few small (p,q) combinations, pick the one with the lowest AIC or BIC, and check that residuals pass the Ljung–Box test. I would also compare candidates on a holdout period, because the model that forecasts best out of sample is the one to deploy. If the series trends or has seasonality, plain ARMA is not enough, and we move to ARIMA or SARIMA.

questions.q: ARIMA stands for:
options: AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average
Automatic Regression with Interval Moving Averages
AutoRegressive Indexed Mean Adjustment
Adjusted Regression Integrated Moving Average
questions.answer: AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average
questions.explanation: AR = autoregressive, I = integrated (differenced), MA = moving average of past errors.

questions.q: In ARIMA(p,d,q), d is:
options: The number of times the series is differenced
The number of lagged forecast errors
The number of lagged values of the series
The seasonal period of the data
questions.answer: The number of times the series is differenced
questions.explanation: d is the order of differencing (integration). Lagged errors are q and lagged values are p.

questions.q: ARIMA(0,1,0) without a constant is:
options: White noise, whose forecasts equal the historical mean
An AR(1) with φ = 0.1
A random walk, whose forecasts equal the last observed value
Simple exponential smoothing with α = 0.5
questions.answer: A random walk, whose forecasts equal the last observed value
questions.explanation: With one difference and no AR/MA terms, Δy_t = ε_t, i.e. y_t = y_{t−1} + ε_t. The naive forecast is the last value, not the mean.

questions.q: The word 'Integrated' in ARIMA refers to:
options: Combining forecasts from several different models
Modelling the differenced series and summing the forecasts back to the original level
Integrating external regressors such as price, promotions and festival dummies into the model
Taking the area under the ACF curve
questions.answer: Modelling the differenced series and summing the forecasts back to the original level
questions.explanation: Integration is the reverse of differencing. Adding external regressors gives ARIMAX, not 'integrated'.

questions.q: ARIMA(1,1,0) means:
options: An AR(1) model fitted to the first differences of the series
An MA(1) model fitted to the first differences of the series
An AR(1) model fitted to the original levels
An AR(1) model with one seasonal difference
questions.answer: An AR(1) model fitted to the first differences of the series
questions.explanation: p = 1, d = 1, q = 0: one AR term on the once-differenced data. An MA(1) on differences would be ARIMA(0,1,1).

questions.q: The Box–Jenkins methodology for ARIMA follows which sequence?
options: Estimation, forecasting, identification, diagnostic checking
Identification, estimation, diagnostic checking, forecasting
Forecasting, identification, estimation, diagnostic checking
Diagnostic checking, estimation, forecasting, identification
questions.answer: Identification, estimation, diagnostic checking, forecasting
questions.explanation: Box–Jenkins first identifies orders (using stationarity checks and ACF/PACF), estimates parameters, checks residuals, then forecasts.

questions.q: ARIMA(0,1,1) produces forecasts equivalent to which method?
options: Holt's linear trend method
Simple exponential smoothing
Holt–Winters seasonal method
A simple moving average of the last three values
questions.answer: Simple exponential smoothing
questions.explanation: ARIMA(0,1,1) and SES give identical point forecasts. Holt's method corresponds to ARIMA(0,2,2).

questions.q: ARIMA models are designed for data that are:
options: Cross-sectional data collected across many customers or stores at one single point in time
Irregularly spaced events with no time ordering
Several series modelled jointly with feedback between them
A single, equally spaced time series that becomes stationary after differencing
questions.answer: A single, equally spaced time series that becomes stationary after differencing
questions.explanation: ARIMA is univariate and needs regular time spacing. Several series with feedback require VAR-type models.

questions.q: How does auto.arima (Hyndman–Khandakar algorithm) choose a model?
options: It always fits ARIMA(1,1,1) to every series
Unit root tests to select d, then a stepwise search over p and q minimising AICc
It selects the model with the highest in-sample R² from all possible orders
It chooses the orders randomly and averages the forecasts
questions.answer: Unit root tests to select d, then a stepwise search over p and q minimising AICc
questions.explanation: auto.arima uses KPSS tests to pick d and AICc to pick p and q. Maximising in-sample R² would favour over-fitting.

questions.q: For a well-specified ARIMA model, the residuals should be:
options: Strongly autocorrelated at lag 1
Trending upward over time
White noise: uncorrelated with zero mean
Equal to the differenced series
questions.answer: White noise: uncorrelated with zero mean
questions.explanation: Remaining autocorrelation means predictable structure was missed. Residuals equal to the differenced series would mean the model explains nothing.

questions.q: A random walk with drift (ARIMA(0,1,0) with constant) has drift 4 per month. The last value is 500. What is the 3-month-ahead forecast?
questions.explanation: ŷ_{T+h} = y_T + h × drift = 500 + 3 × 4 = 512. 504 is only the one-step forecast; 500 ignores the drift.

questions.q: An ARIMA(1,1,0) model is Δy_t = 0.4Δy_{t−1} + ε_t. With y_T = 200 and y_{T−1} = 190, what is ŷ_{T+1}?
questions.explanation: Δy_T = 10, so Δŷ_{T+1} = 0.4 × 10 = 4 and ŷ_{T+1} = 204. Applying 0.4 to the level gives 80; adding the full last change gives 210.

questions.q: ADF on levels gives p = 0.7 and on first differences p = 0.01. The differenced series has an ACF spike at lag 1 only and a decaying PACF. Which model is suggested?
options: ARIMA(1,1,0)
ARIMA(0,0,1)
ARIMA(1,0,1)
ARIMA(0,1,1)
questions.answer: ARIMA(0,1,1)
questions.explanation: One difference is needed (d = 1), and an ACF cut-off at lag 1 indicates MA(1), so q = 1. ARIMA(0,0,1) ignores the unit root.

questions.q: After one difference, a series' PACF has significant spikes at lags 1 and 2 only, and the ACF tails off. Which model is suggested?
options: ARIMA(2,1,0)
ARIMA(0,1,2)
ARIMA(2,0,0)
ARIMA(1,2,0)
questions.answer: ARIMA(2,1,0)
questions.explanation: PACF cut-off at lag 2 on the differenced data means AR(2) with d = 1. ARIMA(0,1,2) would require the ACF to cut off.

questions.q: An ARIMA(0,1,1) model is y_t = y_{t−1} + ε_t + θε_{t−1} with θ = −0.6. If y_T = 120 and ε_T = 10, what is ŷ_{T+1}?
questions.explanation: ŷ_{T+1} = 120 + (−0.6)(10) = 114. Ignoring the negative sign of θ gives 126.

questions.q: An ARIMA model for monthly two-wheeler sales has Ljung–Box p = 0.003 on residuals. What should be done?
options: Use the model, because a small p-value shows the model is highly significant
Increase the forecast horizon to average out the errors
Revise the model, because residual autocorrelation remains
Conclude the series is white noise and stop modelling
questions.answer: Revise the model, because residual autocorrelation remains
questions.explanation: A small Ljung–Box p-value rejects white-noise residuals, so the model has missed structure. It is not a test of model significance.

questions.q: For an ARIMA model with d = 1, how do prediction intervals behave as the horizon grows?
options: They stay the same width at all horizons
They narrow as the horizon increases
They widen steadily with the horizon
They widen only for the first q steps and then stay fixed
questions.answer: They widen steadily with the horizon
questions.explanation: With d ≥ 1, forecast errors accumulate when integrated, so intervals keep widening. Fixed widths after q steps apply to stationary MA models.

questions.q: An ARIMA(0,1,1) has θ = −0.7. What is the equivalent SES smoothing parameter α (using α = 1 + θ)?
questions.explanation: α = 1 + θ = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3. Taking |θ| as α gives 0.7, which reverses the weighting.

questions.q: Can AIC be used to choose between ARIMA(1,0,1) and ARIMA(1,1,1) fitted to the same sales data?
options: No, because differencing changes the data on which the likelihood is computed
Yes, AIC can always compare any two ARIMA models
Yes, but only if both models have the same number of parameters
No, because AIC can only be used for MA models
questions.answer: No, because differencing changes the data on which the likelihood is computed
questions.explanation: Models with different d are fitted to different data, so their likelihoods (and AICs) are not comparable. Choose d first with unit root tests, then compare p and q.

questions.q: An ARIMA(0,2,0) model (no constant) is used. If y_T = 100 and y_{T−1} = 95, what is ŷ_{T+2}?
questions.explanation: With Δ²y = ε, forecasts extend the last change of 5: ŷ_{T+1} = 105 and ŷ_{T+2} = 110. 105 is only the one-step forecast.

questions.q: A colleague picks between ARIMA(2,0,1) with AIC 640 and ARIMA(2,1,1) with AIC 610, concluding that d = 1 is better. What is the flaw?
options: There is no flaw, because the lower AIC always identifies the better model
The flaw is that AIC should be maximised rather than minimised
The flaw is that the two models have different numbers of AR parameters, so AIC cannot compare them
AIC values from models with different orders of differencing are not comparable, so d should be chosen by unit root tests
questions.answer: AIC values from models with different orders of differencing are not comparable, so d should be chosen by unit root tests
questions.explanation: Differencing changes the likelihood's data, invalidating AIC comparisons across d. Different numbers of parameters are fine; AIC is designed for that.

questions.q: For Δy_t = 0.4Δy_{t−1} + ε_t with y_T = 200 and y_{T−1} = 190 (so ŷ_{T+1} = 204), what is ŷ_{T+2}?
For an ARIMA model with d = 1 and a non-zero constant c, long-term forecasts:
options: Converge to the mean of the series
Converge to a fixed non-zero constant
Follow a straight line with a non-zero slope
Follow a quadratic trend
questions.answer: Follow a straight line with a non-zero slope
questions.explanation: In Hyndman's summary, c ≠ 0 with d = 1 gives a linear trend; c ≠ 0 with d = 0 gives the mean; c ≠ 0 with d = 2 gives a quadratic trend.

questions.q: Which ARIMA specification produces long-term forecasts that follow a quadratic trend, which Hyndman & Athanasopoulos warn against?
options: d = 1 with a non-zero constant
d = 2 with a non-zero constant
d = 0 with a non-zero constant
d = 2 with no constant
questions.answer: d = 2 with a non-zero constant
questions.explanation: A constant with two differences implies a quadratic trend. d = 2 without a constant gives a straight line, and d = 1 with a constant also gives a straight line.

questions.q: A new D2C brand has 10 months of sales and wants an ARIMA forecast for annual budgeting. What is the main concern?
options: ARIMA needs at least 10 years of data regardless of frequency
Too few observations to reliably test stationarity, identify orders and estimate parameters
ARIMA cannot be used for any company younger than 5 years
Ten months is ideal, because fewer data points reduce the risk of over-fitting the model's parameters
questions.answer: Too few observations to reliably test stationarity, identify orders and estimate parameters
questions.explanation: Unit root tests and ACF/PACF are unreliable with very short series; simpler methods or judgemental forecasts may be better. There is no fixed '10 years' rule.

questions.q: ARIMA(2,1,0) has AICc 1020.0 and ARIMA(0,1,2) has AICc 1021.5; both pass residual checks. What is the most sensible decision?
options: Reject both, because AICc values above 1000 indicate poor fit
Always choose ARIMA(0,1,2) because MA models forecast better
Average the two AICc values and fit ARIMA(1,1,1) as a compromise between them
Treat them as essentially equivalent and choose by holdout accuracy or simplicity
questions.answer: Treat them as essentially equivalent and choose by holdout accuracy or simplicity
questions.explanation: AICc differences under about 2 are small, so test-set performance or simplicity should decide. The absolute size of AICc is meaningless.

questions.q: An ARIMA model is fitted to log(monthly sales). The point forecast of log sales is 6.0. What is the forecast in original units (median)?
questions.explanation: Back-transform with the exponential: e⁶ ≈ 403.4. 10⁶ assumes base-10 logs; leaving 6.0 forgets to back-transform.

questions.q: A retailer's ARIMA fits pre-2020 data well, but COVID lockdowns created a sharp, temporary collapse in 2020. What is the best way to handle this?
options: Ignore it, because ARIMA automatically treats outliers as noise
Model the disruption explicitly, e.g. with intervention dummies (ARIMAX), or adjust the data before fitting
Increase the differencing order to d = 3 so that the extra differencing automatically absorbs both the collapse and the recovery
Drop all data after 2019 permanently, even for future model updates and forecasts
questions.answer: Model the disruption explicitly, e.g. with intervention dummies (ARIMAX), or adjust the data before fitting
questions.explanation: ARIMA assumes stable dynamics; large one-off shocks distort parameters unless handled with interventions or adjustments. Extra differencing does not fix a one-off break.

questions.q: An ARIMA(0,1,1) for weekly demand is estimated with θ = −0.95. What does this imply about the forecasts?
options: They behave like a naive forecast that copies the last value
They behave like SES with α ≈ 0.05, reacting very slowly to new data
They behave like SES with α ≈ 0.95, reacting almost fully to new data
They are explosive because |θ| is close to 1
questions.answer: They behave like SES with α ≈ 0.05, reacting very slowly to new data
questions.explanation: α = 1 + θ = 0.05, so forecasts change very little each week. Confusing α with |θ| leads to the 0.95 distractor.

questions.q: The planning head asks whether to replace an existing Holt–Winters model with ARIMA for monthly FMCG demand. What is the best approach?
options: Switch to ARIMA, because it is always more accurate than exponential smoothing
Keep Holt–Winters, because ARIMA cannot handle any seasonality
Choose whichever model has the lower AIC, even though the two models are fitted to differently transformed data
Compare both on the same holdout or rolling-origin evaluation and adopt the one with lower forecast error
questions.answer: Compare both on the same holdout or rolling-origin evaluation and adopt the one with lower forecast error
questions.explanation: ARIMA and ETS families overlap and neither dominates; out-of-sample comparison decides. AIC is not comparable across these model classes when data are transformed or differenced differently.

references: ARIMA stands for AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average and is written ARIMA(p,d,q). Because most business series have trends, we first difference the data d times to make it stationary; that is the 'integrated' part. On the differenced data we fit p autoregressive terms, which use past values, and q moving-average terms, which use past forecast errors. We choose d with unit root tests like ADF or KPSS, and p and q from the ACF and PACF or by minimising AIC. Forecasts of the differences are summed back to the original level. Special cases include ARIMA(0,1,0), the random walk, and ARIMA(0,1,1), which matches simple exponential smoothing. The residuals should be white noise.

Suppose we forecast monthly two-wheeler sales that have grown steadily. The ADF test fails to reject a unit root, so we take first differences, the monthly changes, which pass the test, giving d = 1. The ACF of the changes has one spike at lag 1 and the PACF decays, so we fit ARIMA(0,1,1). We check the residual ACF and Ljung–Box test to confirm nothing is left over, then forecast. The model forecasts next month's change and adds it to the latest sales figure. Because uncertainty from each future change accumulates, the prediction interval widens the further ahead we look, which is important for setting inventory ranges.

For managers, ARIMA is a flexible, data-driven way to forecast a single series using only its own history, which is useful when we have no good drivers to model. Its strength is that it handles trends through differencing and short-term dynamics through AR and MA terms, and tools like auto.arima automate the selection with AICc. The decisions that matter are the order of differencing, keeping the model simple and validating it out of sample against alternatives like exponential smoothing. ARIMA has limits: it needs a reasonable amount of history, assumes the pattern stays stable, and needs explicit handling of events like GST or COVID, and a seasonal extension for festive cycles.

questions.q: In SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)s notation, s represents:
options: The seasonal period, i.e. the number of observations per seasonal cycle
The number of seasonal differences applied
The seasonal moving-average order
The standard deviation of the seasonal component
questions.answer: The seasonal period, i.e. the number of observations per seasonal cycle
questions.explanation: s is the length of the seasonal cycle (e.g. 12 for monthly data). The number of seasonal differences is D.

questions.q: For monthly data with an annual pattern, the seasonal period s is:
questions.explanation: There are 12 months in a yearly cycle. 4 is for quarterly data, 7 for daily data with a weekly cycle and 52 for weekly data.

questions.q: In SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)s, D is:
options: The number of seasonal differences
The number of ordinary differences
The seasonal AR order
The number of seasons in the data
questions.answer: The number of seasonal differences
questions.explanation: D counts seasonal differences (y_t − y_{t−s}); d counts ordinary differences.

questions.q: In SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)s, P is:
options: The seasonal moving-average order
The non-seasonal AR order
The seasonal period
The seasonal autoregressive order
questions.answer: The seasonal autoregressive order
questions.explanation: P is the number of seasonal AR terms at lags s, 2s, ... Q is the seasonal MA order and p the non-seasonal AR order.

questions.q: SARIMA is preferred over ARIMA when:
options: The series has a trend but no seasonal pattern of any kind
The series shows a repeating seasonal pattern, such as festive or monthly peaks
The data are cross-sectional rather than time-ordered
Several related series must be modelled jointly
questions.answer: The series shows a repeating seasonal pattern, such as festive or monthly peaks
questions.explanation: SARIMA adds seasonal terms to capture repeating patterns. Trend alone is handled by ordinary differencing in ARIMA.

questions.q: For quarterly data, the seasonal period s is:
questions.explanation: Four quarters make one annual cycle. 12 is for monthly data.

questions.q: With D = 1 and s = 12, the seasonal difference is:
questions.explanation: A seasonal difference subtracts the same month of the previous year. y_t − y_{t−1} is an ordinary difference.

questions.q: SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 is widely known as the:
options: Random walk model
Airline model
Holt–Winters additive model
Seasonal naive model
questions.answer: Airline model
questions.explanation: Box and Jenkins popularised it using the international airline passengers data. The seasonal naive model is SARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,0)s.

questions.q: In a monthly SARIMA model, a seasonal MA(1) term links the current value to:
options: The observed value 12 months earlier
The error (shock) from 12 months earlier
The error from 1 month earlier
The average of the last 12 months
questions.answer: The error (shock) from 12 months earlier
questions.explanation: A seasonal MA term uses ε_{t−12}. Linking to the observed value y_{t−12} would be a seasonal AR term.

questions.q: A quick-commerce firm has daily order data with a strong weekday/weekend pattern. Which seasonal period suits SARIMA?
questions.explanation: The weekly cycle repeats every 7 days. 365 would capture an annual cycle, which SARIMA handles poorly for daily data.

questions.q: In the ACF of a seasonally differenced monthly series, there is a significant spike at lag 12 only (none at 24, 36), while the PACF decays across lags 12, 24, 36. What is suggested?
options: Seasonal MA(1): Q = 1
Seasonal AR(1): P = 1
Seasonal MA(2): Q = 2
No seasonal terms are needed
questions.answer: Seasonal MA(1): Q = 1
questions.explanation: A single seasonal ACF spike with decaying seasonal PACF mirrors the MA signature at seasonal lags. The reverse pattern would indicate P = 1.

questions.q: A monthly series' PACF has a significant spike at lag 12 only, while the ACF decays across lags 12, 24, 36. What is suggested?
options: Seasonal MA(1): Q = 1
Non-seasonal AR(12): p = 12
Seasonal AR(1): P = 1
A second seasonal difference: D = 2
questions.answer: Seasonal AR(1): P = 1
questions.explanation: A seasonal PACF cut-off at lag 12 with decaying seasonal ACF points to P = 1. p = 12 would add 12 non-seasonal terms unnecessarily.

questions.q: How many ARMA coefficients (excluding constant and error variance) does SARIMA(1,1,1)(1,1,1)12 estimate?
questions.explanation: φ1, θ1, Φ1 and Θ1 make 4; the differences d and D add no parameters. Counting d and D as parameters gives 6.

questions.q: Ten years of monthly data (120 observations) are modelled with d = 1 and D = 1, s = 12. How many observations remain after differencing?
questions.explanation: The seasonal difference loses 12 and the ordinary difference loses 1, so 120 − 13 = 107. 108 forgets the ordinary difference.

questions.q: Monthly hotel occupancy in Goa rises steadily over the years and peaks every October–January. Which differencing is most likely needed?
options: d = 1 and D = 1
d = 0 and D = 0
d = 2 and D = 0
d = 0 and D = 2
questions.answer: d = 1 and D = 1
questions.explanation: The trend calls for an ordinary difference and the strong annual pattern for a seasonal difference. Two ordinary differences would not remove seasonality.

questions.q: What is the forecast for next July from SARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,0)12?
options: The value from last month
The average of the last 12 months
Zero, since no AR or MA terms are present
The value from last July
questions.answer: The value from last July
questions.explanation: With only a seasonal difference, y_t = y_{t−12} + ε_t, which is the seasonal naive method. The last month's value would come from ARIMA(0,1,0).

questions.q: After fitting ARIMA(1,1,1) to monthly sales, the residual ACF shows significant spikes at lags 12 and 24. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Add seasonal terms, i.e. move to a SARIMA model with s = 12
Increase p to 24
Remove the MA term from the model
Accept the model, because spikes at lags 12 and 24 are always just random noise
questions.answer: Add seasonal terms, i.e. move to a SARIMA model with s = 12
questions.explanation: Residual spikes at seasonal lags reveal unmodelled seasonality. Increasing p to 24 is far less parsimonious than seasonal terms.

questions.q: A SARIMA(0,0,0)(1,0,0)12 with Φ = 0.5 and mean zero is fitted to sales deviations. Last March was 40 above the mean. What is the forecast deviation for this March?
questions.explanation: ŷ = Φ × y_{t−12} = 0.5 × 40 = 20. Copying 40 corresponds to seasonal naive (Φ = 1).

questions.q: In the airline model SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12, which terms are included?
options: One AR term, one seasonal AR term and no differencing at all
Two ordinary differences and two MA terms
One ordinary difference, one seasonal difference, one AR term and one seasonal AR term
One ordinary difference, one seasonal difference, one MA term and one seasonal MA term
questions.answer: One ordinary difference, one seasonal difference, one MA term and one seasonal MA term
questions.explanation: (0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 means d = 1, q = 1, D = 1, Q = 1 with no AR terms. Confusing MA with AR terms gives the last distractor.

questions.q: A SARIMA(0,1,0)(0,1,0)12 forecasts ŷ_{T+1} = y_T + y_{T−11} − y_{T−12}. Sales were 300 in December 2025, 250 in January 2025 and 280 in December 2024. What is the January 2026 forecast?
questions.explanation: ŷ = 300 + 250 − 280 = 270: last January's level adjusted by the latest year-on-year change (+20). 330 adds the change with the wrong sign (300 + 280 − 250).

questions.q: In SARIMA(1,0,0)(1,0,0)12 with φ = 0.5 and Φ = 0.4, (1 − 0.5B)(1 − 0.4B¹²)y_t = ε_t. What is the coefficient on y_{t−13} in the expanded equation for y_t?
questions.explanation: Expanding gives 1 − 0.5B − 0.4B¹² + 0.2B¹³, so y_t = 0.5y_{t−1} + 0.4y_{t−12} − 0.2y_{t−13} + ε_t. The sign flips when moving the term to the right-hand side.

questions.q: In an airline model with θ = −0.4 and Θ = −0.6, the MA part is (1 + θB)(1 + ΘB¹²)ε_t. What is the coefficient on ε_{t−13}?
questions.explanation: θΘ = (−0.4)(−0.6) = +0.24. The multiplicative form creates this lag-13 term automatically, which is why spikes appear at lags 11 and 13 too.

questions.q: The ACF of a differenced monthly series shows significant spikes at lags 1, 11, 12 and 13. Which model structure explains this pattern most parsimoniously?
options: A non-seasonal MA(13) with all thirteen MA coefficients estimated freely
SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12, whose multiplicative MA terms create spikes around lag 12
SARIMA(1,1,0)(1,1,0)12 with seasonal AR terms only
White noise, because spikes at 11 and 13 are not at the seasonal lag
questions.answer: SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12, whose multiplicative MA terms create spikes around lag 12
questions.explanation: Multiplying (1 + θB)(1 + ΘB¹²) produces correlation at lags 11 and 13 as well as 1 and 12. MA(13) would use 13 parameters to do what two can.

questions.q: A retailer has weekly sales with an annual cycle (s ≈ 52.18). Why is SARIMA awkward here, and what is a better approach?
options: SARIMA works perfectly with s = 52, so no other approach is needed
Aggregate to daily data and use s = 7, since this captures the annual cycle
Use SARIMA with s = 4, because there are four weeks in a month
s is long and non-integer, so seasonal terms are hard to estimate; use Fourier terms in a dynamic harmonic regression
questions.answer: s is long and non-integer, so seasonal terms are hard to estimate; use Fourier terms in a dynamic harmonic regression
questions.explanation: Long, fractional seasonal periods make seasonal differencing and lags unwieldy; Fourier terms with ARMA errors handle them smoothly (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos).

questions.q: Hourly electricity demand for a Mumbai utility has both daily (24) and weekly (168) cycles. What is the key limitation of SARIMA?
options: SARIMA handles only one seasonal period, so multiple seasonality needs approaches like Fourier terms, TBATS or MSTL
SARIMA can include any number of seasonal periods directly in its notation
SARIMA cannot be used for hourly data under any circumstances
SARIMA requires s to be less than 12, so both cycles are too long to model
questions.answer: SARIMA handles only one seasonal period, so multiple seasonality needs approaches like Fourier terms, TBATS or MSTL
questions.explanation: Standard SARIMA has a single s. Multiple-seasonality methods (Fourier regressors, TBATS, MSTL) are designed for such data.

questions.q: An analyst proposes SARIMA(1,1,1)(1,2,1)12 for monthly sales. What is the main concern?
options: D = 2 is the standard choice for monthly data, so nothing needs to change
The model has too few AR terms to capture the trend
D = 2 (and d + D = 3) is very rarely needed and usually means over-differencing, inflating forecast variance
The seasonal period should be 24 when D = 2
questions.answer: D = 2 (and d + D = 3) is very rarely needed and usually means over-differencing, inflating forecast variance
questions.explanation: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos advise D ≤ 1 and d + D ≤ 2 in practice; more differencing adds noise and unrealistic forecast behaviour.

questions.q: For a SARIMA model with d = 1, D = 1 and no constant, what pattern do long-horizon forecasts follow?
options: A flat line at the historical mean with no seasonal pattern
A seasonal pattern that fades to zero over time
The seasonal pattern repeats around a level that continues the recent trend
Explosive growth that accelerates every year
questions.answer: The seasonal pattern repeats around a level that continues the recent trend
questions.explanation: With both ordinary and seasonal differencing, forecasts keep the seasonal shape and extrapolate the trend. A flat mean forecast comes from a stationary model.

questions.q: A new D2C brand has only 18 months of monthly sales and wants a SARIMA(1,1,1)(1,1,1)12. What is the main problem?
options: 18 months is plenty, because SARIMA needs just one full cycle of data
SARIMA needs exactly 24 months of data, and having more than that also reduces accuracy
After seasonal and ordinary differencing only 5 observations remain, far too few to estimate seasonal terms
The model needs s = 18 to match the length of the data
questions.answer: After seasonal and ordinary differencing only 5 observations remain, far too few to estimate seasonal terms
questions.explanation: 18 − 12 − 1 = 5 differenced observations cannot support identification or estimation. Simpler or judgement-based methods are safer until more history exists.

questions.q: A soft-drink brand's monthly seasonal pattern is very stable year after year. Why might seasonal differencing be inappropriate, and what is an alternative?
options: Seasonal differencing is always required whenever any seasonal pattern can be seen in the data
Stable seasonality makes the series non-stationary, so D = 2 is needed
Stable (deterministic) seasonality can be over-differenced; use seasonal dummies or Fourier terms with ARMA errors
Stable seasonality should be ignored, since it adds no forecasting information
questions.answer: Stable (deterministic) seasonality can be over-differenced; use seasonal dummies or Fourier terms with ARMA errors
questions.explanation: Seasonal differencing assumes stochastic seasonality; a fixed pattern is better captured deterministically. Over-differencing creates a near non-invertible seasonal MA term.

questions.q: A SARIMA(0,1,0)(0,1,0)12 is fitted to monthly hotel revenue. Revenue was 520 in March 2026, 480 in April 2025 and 450 in March 2025. What is the April 2026 forecast (ŷ = y_{T} + y_{T−11} − y_{T−12})?
questions.explanation: ŷ = 520 + 480 − 450 = 550: last April plus the latest year-on-year change (+70). 490 applies the change with the wrong sign, 480 is the seasonal naive value that ignores the trend, and 590 adds the change to March instead of last April.

references: Seasonal ARIMA, or SARIMA, extends ARIMA to series with a repeating seasonal pattern. It is written SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)s. The first bracket is the usual non-seasonal part: AR order p, differencing d and MA order q. The second bracket is the seasonal part at lags of s, where s is the season length, such as 12 for monthly or 4 for quarterly data. D is the number of seasonal differences, like y_t − y_{t−12}, and P and Q are seasonal AR and MA terms that link this month to the same month last year. We identify seasonal orders from ACF and PACF spikes at lags s, 2s and so on, and check the residuals are white noise.

Think of monthly sales at an Indian apparel retailer, which rise every October–November for Diwali and grow year on year. A plain ARIMA misses the festive pattern, leaving residual spikes at lag 12. With SARIMA I would take one ordinary difference for the growth and one seasonal difference, comparing each month with the same month last year. If the ACF of the differenced data shows spikes at lags 1 and 12, an airline model, SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12, is a natural choice. Its forecasts reproduce the festive peak each year on top of the trend, which helps plan inventory, staffing and marketing spend ahead of the season.

For managers, SARIMA is the tool to use when demand has a predictable calendar rhythm, monthly, quarterly or weekly, and we want forecasts that respect both trend and seasonality. The key decisions are the seasonal period s, whether to apply a seasonal difference (rarely more than one), and keeping the seasonal and non-seasonal orders small to avoid over-fitting, using AICc and a holdout test. We should know its limits: it needs several years of history, it handles only one seasonal period, and very long periods like 52 weeks or multiple cycles in hourly data are better handled with Fourier terms or other methods. Residual checks confirm the seasonal pattern has been fully captured.
